#3285. Energy Fuels (UUUU) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Pinyon Plain ore grades disappointed, but uranium profits held steady.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Energy Fuels Inc. (UUUU -8.22%) reported third quarter results as the company executed on its strategy to build a fully integrated Western rare earth supply chain. Management stated that the acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials has added metallization and alloy making capabilities to its operations, while progress continues toward a final investment decision for the Donald Project. The company reported a net loss for the period primarily due to noncash valuation changes in its investment portfolio, while its uranium segment remained profitable for the third consecutive quarter. Management indicated that operational adjustments at the Pinyon Plain mine are addressing earlier grade issues to support future uranium production.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you all for joining us for Energy Fuels Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, today's session is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to turn the floor over to Kim Casey, Director of Investor Relations. The floor is yours.

Kim Casey: Good morning, and thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. Presenting today are Ross Bhappu, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Nate Bennett, Chief Financial Officer. Our earnings news release and today's slide presentation are available on the Investors section of our website under the Presentations tab. And a replay of today's discussion will also be available on the website through the Events link. During today's call, management may make forward-looking statements. All forward-looking statements are based on current assumptions and beliefs as of today. Such statements are subject to risks and uncertainties and for a detailed list of such risks please refer to the Risk Factors section within Energy Fuels 10-Qs and 10-Ks filed with the SEC.

Energy Fuels is under no obligation to publicly update forward-looking statements after the date of this call, except as otherwise required by applicable law. I would now like to turn the call over to the President and CEO of Energy Fuels, Ross Bhappu.

Ross Bhappu: Well, thank you, Kim. Last quarter, I told you that our story was one of execution. This quarter, I'm very pleased to tell you about several important steps we've taken to advance on that path. On August 28, we closed on the acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials, ASM. During the third quarter, we continued to advance the proposed acquisition of Vacuumschmelze or as I'll refer to it during the presentation, VAC. At the White Mesa Mill, we qualified our heavy rare earth oxide production with a major global permanent magnet manufacturer, and we approved commencement of construction of our Phase 1B and 1C heavy rare earths expansion as well as our MREC processing operations.

Finally, we received conditional government loan commitments for our Donald Project and continued successfully moving this valuable project toward a final investment decision, which we hope to make by the end of the year. There's still a lot of work ahead of us, but quarter-by-quarter, we're putting the pieces of our strategy together and advancing our goal of building a fully integrated rare earth mine to magnet supply chain, which we expect to achieve soon. While we successfully execute on our rare earth strategy, we also continue to drive revenue from uranium sales, and we're readying ourselves for future uranium expansion as we believe the demand for uranium will increase and with the commodity prices.

With respect to our uranium business, we experienced some lower grades in the mined areas of Pinyon Plain Mine, which affected our contained U3O8 yellowcake totals for Q3. However, we've made some adjustments to our operations, and we expect to see improvements in grade and future production, which should get our mined contained U3O8 totals back on track. I'll come back to uranium in just a few minutes. But first, let me start with ASM. ASM, Australian Strategic Materials, we closed on this acquisition in late August, and I'm very pleased to officially welcome the ASM team to Energy Fuels. ASM is an important component because it gives Energy Fuels a capability we simply did not have before.

ASM takes us into metallization and alloy making, one of the critical pinch points in the global rare earth magnet supply chain. Importantly, ASM brings Energy Fuels an operating facility in Ochang, South Korea, just south of Seoul, that's actively producing and selling neodymium and iron-boron rare earth to magnet manufacturers today, including VAC. Furthermore, capacity expansions are currently underway at the Korean plant with new furnaces and a new strip caster being installed as we speak. ASM and now Energy Fuels plans to build a new metal and alloy plant here in the U.S. when the time is right.

The ASM acquisition also brings to us the Dubbo Project in Australia, which could become another near-term source of rare earth feedstock for the White Mesa Mill. I recently visited ASM's operations in Australia and Korea, and I came away more excited about the acquisition than ever. The early integration is going well as the local teams and technical experts have not missed a step with the transition. This is exactly the point of our acquisition strategy. Rather than developing metal and alloy magnet manufacturing capabilities internally, we're adding commercial facilities, technical capabilities and customers at scale and in rapid time.

The Korea metals plant has existing capacity of 1,300 tonnes per year of neodymium-iron-boron alloy along with existing commercial metallization capabilities for neodymium and praseodymium. The plant is currently being expanded to increase neodymium-iron-boron alloy capability to 3,600 tonnes per year, which is expected to be commissioned early in 2027. While I was visiting the plant a few weeks ago, we have just taken delivery of a new strip casting machine that's now in the process of being installed. We continue to produce metals and alloys and sell them to fulfill commitments we inherited from our ASM. This offers direct revenue until we're able to transition to feed our own magnet manufacturing with the planned VAC acquisition.

Our focus now is on execution, scaling operations and capturing additional value across the supply chain. ASM establishes our platform in metals and alloys. VAC will take us the final step downstream into highly sought-after finished rare earth magnets. We continue to work through the appropriate applicable regulatory processes and still anticipate that the VAC transaction will close early in 2027. I also want to directly address another topic regarding VAC and provide some context for investors. A few weeks ago, news came out that there was a dispute with a large customer of VAC Sumter, South Carolina facility. Some inaccurate and incomplete investor narratives have been developed. So please allow me a few minutes to set the record straight.

Energy Fuels knew of the Sumter customer dispute before signing the VAC acquisition agreement. Indeed, the dispute was reflected in the transaction structure, pricing and economics. Purchase price adjustments could be implemented depending on the outcome of the arbitration between VAC and its customer. An arbitration result below the agreed assumptions is expected to reduce the acquisition price, while the result above them benefits VAC and of course, after closing will benefit Energy Fuels. Our internal valuations and projections excluded current and future revenue and EBITDA from this customer and the related offtake. The dispute, therefore, does not change Energy Fuels valuation assumptions and rationale for the acquisition. The Sumter facility has capacity to fulfill the existing agreement.

And if it does not continue on those terms, that capacity can be used to support new customer contracts. While we may need to expend some capital to meet new customer requirements, which is again reflected in our valuation, we firmly believe there is considerable demand for Sumter's rare earth magnets and processing capabilities. In addition, I'd like to stress we have no concerns about VAC's technical abilities, customer base and the ability to produce rare earth permanent magnets to customer qualifications and specifications. The Sumter plant is brand new. It's a state-of-the-art facility, highly robotic, and it's located right here in the United States. I believe it's important to reiterate that VAC has approximately 1,000 existing customers.

They've been making rare earth permanent magnets for over 40 years, and they've delivered over 1 billion rare earth permanent magnets over the past decade. They know what they're doing. They're highly qualified and they're a highly unique company, and they remain the clear Western leader in the production of rare earth permanent magnets. Demand for neodymium-iron-boron magnets across the globe is expected to grow by more than 50% over the next decade with Europe and North America being key demand growth drivers. VAC brings established manufacturing expertise and when combined with ASM, it will give us capabilities spanning metals, alloys and finished magnets.

In addition, we disclosed a bit of housekeeping with an updated $500 million prospectus supplement for our existing ATM program. The program preserves flexibility to issue equity selectively and when market conditions and the stock price warrant. We've used an ATM in the past for many years, and we have a long track record of strong fiscal discipline in using it. We intend to remain disciplined in using this one. That brings us back to our upstream operations. If we're going to build a meaningful downstream magnet business, we need the ability to supply it with a secure source of feed. To that end, we continue to advance the Donald joint venture project in Australia.

A big milestone was reached last week when we announced receipt of a conditional commitment with the Export Finance Australia and the Australian National Reconstruction Fund Corporation for AUD 180 million of a proposed AUD 200 million senior project debt facility. The remaining AUD 20 million commitment will be coming from commercial banks. As we continue to work closely with relevant government financing authorities and we finalize term sheets, those discussions have been constructive, and we remain on track for a final investment decision by year-end. Together with our heavy mineral sands asset, Donald is intended to establish a reliable, long-duration source of feedstock for our rare earth business.

Importantly, the Donald Project is an excellent source of heavy rare earth minerals and is very high in dysprosium and terbium in particular. These are key ingredients for producing high-performance rare earth permanent magnets. As we move forward in developing our raw material feedstock, we're also making preparations to expand our commercial scale of rare earth processing capacity at the White Mesa Mill. During the quarter, we approved commencement of construction on our Phase 1B and 1C heavy rare earth expansion. Once operational, Energy Fuels will have the commercial scale light and heavy rare earth production capacity.

Just as importantly, the expansion will include an MREC, mixed rare earth carbonate, circuit that will allow us to process uranium and rare earth simultaneously, something we can't do today. Today, we have to decide whether to produce rare earths or uranium in campaigning the mill. When the expansion is complete, we expect to have a significantly greater flexibility to produce both rare earths and uranium simultaneously. The White Mesa Mill is ultimately intended to become the bridge between our feedstock assets upstream and our metals, alloys and magnet manufacturing operations downstream. That flexibility matters.

As the downstream business grows, we'll be able to make thoughtful decisions about where our capacity creates the greatest value based on market conditions, economics and the needs of our business. So when you step back and look at what we're putting together, the logic is quite clear, feedstock, processing and separation, metals and alloys, the ultimately -- and ultimately, the finished magnets. We are truly creating a fully integrated minded magnet company. Each piece has an important role, and our job now is to execute and put those pieces -- get those pieces working together. As you can see, we're making tremendous progress. Now let me turn to uranium.

Uranium remains the core business for Energy Fuels and an important operating and financial foundation for the company. We're seeing upward movement in the uranium pricing in both the spot and the term markets as supply and demand fundamentals are taking shape. During the quarter, we mined 385,000 pounds at our operations, but we didn't process any uranium at the mill. That was idled for planned maintenance and rebuilding of our stockpiles and feedstock. Please recall that the mill processes ore and mineralized material faster than we are currently mining it.

As a result, and as a further reminder, we met our planned 2026 finished uranium production guidance by the end of the second quarter, and we're well inventoried to fulfill next year's contract commitments while potentially selling opportunistically on the spot market. We ended the third quarter with approximately 2.4 million pounds of combined ore mineralized material in processed and finished uranium inventory. To be clear, the ore grades at Pinyon Plain came in below our expectations this quarter. In response, we deployed an overnight crew to double our efforts in the quantity mined and are now seeing improvements in total production. You may recall the Pinyon Plain is a small underground breccia pipe mine. These formations are quite unique.

They're very high-grade deposits, which are mined differently than other uranium mines. Due mainly to Pinyon Plain, Energy Fuels remains the largest U.S. producer and one of the lowest cost sources of yellowcake U3O8 in the world. As we look to the future, we continue to progress our domestic uranium production and bring additional assets online as the Pinyon Plain production is expected to decline in coming years. As part of that effort, we've advanced 4 of our pipeline projects, including the Whirlwind, Pandora, Bullfrog and Roca Honda projects.

And of course, Nichols Ranch is still there sitting on care and maintenance and can quickly be called into service when economic environment improves to the point that we can maintain margins for production. The Whirlwind mine has seen activity this quarter, including current dewatering and plans to reopen next year. Bullfrog, Pandora and Roca Honda permitting has progressed, and we continue to move those projects forward. These 4 assets, Nichols Ranch and others in our pipeline can complement our existing uranium operations and give us production capacity as demand for the U.S. uranium market grows. Now let me spend just a minute on our balance sheet and capital. We're executing an ambitious and capital-intensive plan.

We're not shy about this fact. Indeed, it energizes our team every day as we believe we are well down the road towards capturing highly unique and valuable market opportunities. The important point is that we're starting from a position of strength with multiple funding sources already in process, which gives us flexibility in how we fund our growth. We ended the quarter with approximately $932 million in working capital and total revenue of $29.2 million. Our results this quarter also reflect several onetime operational and transactional-related items, which Nate is going to walk you through here in greater detail.

As we finance our growth, we have several sources of capital available to us, including our balance sheet, several government funding sources, our term loan facility, our ATM program and other conventional financing alternatives. We will evaluate those funding options as well as the viability and timing of actual asset development and project -- on a project-by-project basis. We will not progress a project and expansion or a funding source if it's not advantageous or accretive. Our objective is simply not to fund growth, but it's to fund the right growth at the right time and in a way that we believe creates the greatest long-term value.

When I look back at the quarter, I'm encouraged by the progress we've made. ASM is now part of Energy Fuels and operating today. Donald is nearing FID. White Mesa is efficiently processing uranium and the heavy rare earth processing expansion is advancing. We continue to work towards closing on the VAC acquisition. And despite some operational challenges this quarter, our uranium business continues to deliver. There's still a lot of work ahead of us, but the path is clear. Last quarter, I said our story was about execution, and that hasn't changed. Quarter-by-quarter, we're moving the strategy from plants on paper to operating assets.

We're building the capabilities that we believe are necessary to establish a fully integrated Western rare earth supply chain while continuing to grow our uranium business. That's what execution looks like, and that's what remains our key focus. Now I'd like to turn the presentation over to Nate Bennett for our financial results. Nate?

Nathan Bennett: Thanks, Ross. Before I get into the numbers, I encourage everyone to review today's discussion alongside our Form 10-Q and other public filings as those documents provide additional detail and context around our results, risk factors and related disclosures. As we continue to grow and diversify the business, it's important to remember that we manage and evaluate our operations by commodity line. Today, that primarily includes uranium, while our rare earth and heavy mineral sands, metals, alloys and magnet businesses continue to advance through development activities. Turning to our financial results. Energy Fuels continues to have a solid foundation.

As of September 30, 2026, we had approximately $932 million of working capital and $1.7 billion of total assets, which provides us with a strong foundation for our strategic growth initiatives and allows us to be flexible in our projects as we put capital to work. During the third quarter, we reported a net loss of $52.2 million or $0.20 per share. The loss was driven primarily by $35.3 million of noncash unrealized mark-to-market losses on our marketable securities. At the same time, our investment portfolio generated $9.4 million of cash interest income during the quarter, which partially offset the unrealized valuation loss.

The majority of our marketable securities are interest-bearing debt securities, primarily U.S. treasury bills and government agency bonds. During the quarter, higher market interest rates put downward pressure on bond values. And because these securities are carried at fair value, those market movements resulted in unrealized losses. Importantly, these losses did not represent a current cash outflow. We are excited to highlight that our uranium segment remained profitable for the third straight quarter. The weighted average realized price per pound of U3O8 sold also rose for the third consecutive quarter, increasing 10% from Q2 and 27% from Q1, while operating cost per pound and cost of goods sold remained steady. Turning to our operating results.

Performance benefited from improved realized uranium pricing and higher margins on uranium sales. SG&A was $18.3 million during the quarter, with the year-over-year increase primarily reflecting higher personnel costs and the inclusion of approximately 1 month of ASM following the acquisition. We also incurred $9 million of transaction and integration-related costs associated with the ASM acquisition and pending VAC acquisition. Our uranium segment generated $28.7 million of revenue and $17.9 million of gross profit, representing gross margin of approximately 63%. We sold 320,000 pounds at an average realized price of $88.90 per pound, while our weighted average cost applicable to uranium revenues was approximately $34 per pound.

The uranium segment continued to generate positive operating income, helping to support our exploration and development activities and corporate costs. This steady quarter-over-quarter performance highlights the resilience of our uranium business, reinforces our position as the leading U.S. uranium platform and provides a strong foundation for our strategic growth plans across our businesses. In contrast, the losses incurred with our rare earth elements and heavy mineral sand businesses primarily reflect planned developments to advance projects, including Vara Mada, Donald and Bahia toward future production. These investments include drilling, engineering, permitting, infrastructure, development and organizational growth. We closed the ASM acquisition on August 28, and therefore, our third quarter results include only a limited contribution from ASM.

In the near term, we intend to take a disciplined approach to utilization of the Korean Metals Plant as we focus on completing the planned expansion. As such, we expect ASM's contributions to our financials to be limited over the near term. Over time, we expect that contribution to build as the individual components of our mine-to-magnet strategy come online, including ASM, VAC, Donald and additional feedstock sources. As these pieces come together, we expect to be better positioned to realize the Korean Metals Plant's expanded capacity and drive a more meaningful contribution to our operating and financial results. Turning to uranium. The segment generated strong revenue during the quarter.

Pinyon Plain ore grades averaged 1.04% during the third quarter, which improved meaningfully from 0.71% in the second quarter as we continue to progress through the ore body. While the improvement has taken longer than we initially anticipated as mining transitions between higher grade zones, the trend is positive, and we expect grades to continue to improve as we advance through the current mining zones and ultimately into the Juniper Zone. Year-to-date, we have mined approximately 1.1 million pounds of contained U3O8. As Ross mentioned, we have added an overnight crew at Pinyon Plain, effectively doubling the number of operating shifts, and we expect grades to improve as mining progresses through the current mining zones and into the Juniper Zone.

Turning to costs. Our Finish U3O8 inventory carried a weighted average cost of approximately $34 per pound as of September 30, broadly in line with the end of the second quarter and down from approximately $36 per pound at the end of the first quarter. Our finished inventory reflects production and purchases from various sources over time and does not yet fully reflect the recently mined Pinyon Plain ore, which has not been fully processed. The Pinyon Plain ore processed in the most recent mill run had a weighted average cost of approximately $23 per pound. As this lower cost material is processed and moves into finished inventory, we expect it to benefit our overall uranium inventory cost profile.

We believe this low-cost production base provides us with a meaningful competitive advantage as we continue to grow our uranium business. The mill completed planned maintenance during the third quarter, and we currently expect the next uranium processing run to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026 or early 2027 as we continue mining and building our ore and mineralized material stockpiles. Our uranium inventory remains a significant strategic asset, providing flexibility to meet customer commitments while supporting our long-term strategy to build a fully integrated critical minerals platform.

With approximately 2.4 million pounds of U3O8 at quarter end, we have the flexibility to fulfill long-term contract deliveries, pursue spot sales when market conditions warrant and manage the timing of production and sales to maximize value. As we move through the remainder of the year, our focus remains on executing our uranium production plan and positioning the business for continued growth. Turning to our 2026 guidance, as shown on this slide, we have already achieved the low end of our full year guidance for processed pounds and remain on track to achieve the low end of our full year guidance ranges for sales.

We remain hopeful that the additional shift in higher grades at Pinyon Plain will help us reach the low end of our mining guidance. Our uranium operations continue to provide a strong economic foundation for the company, supported by attractive market fundamentals and the value generated across our production and sales activities. Overall, we continue to advance our uranium operations, maintain a competitive cost structure and reinforce our position as a leading U.S.-based uranium producer. The progress across our operations, coupled with the significant production potential of our existing asset base provides a solid foundation for expanding our capabilities, capturing future opportunities and strengthening our presence across the nuclear, energy and critical minerals markets.

And with that, I'll turn it back to Ross.

Ross Bhappu: Thank you, Nate, for that summary. With that, I'd like to conclude with a few comments and summarize the milestones we've accomplished and where we are as we head toward the end of 2026. Looking ahead, our priority is to make the pieces of our strategy work together. At the White Mesa Mill, the heavy rare earth expansion and terbium oxide qualification provide a foundation for advancing our production capabilities. With ASM now part of Energy Fuels, our focus is on integrating and scaling our metals and alloys operations. The proposed VAC acquisition, subject to regulatory approvals, will extend Energy Fuels platform into finished rare earth magnets.

Our goal is not simply to own assets across the supply chain, but to build and connect a scalable business from mine to magnets. That means advancing the Donald Project from conditional financing toward a final investment decision while continuing the permitting and government work needed to support a future investment decision at Vara Mada. We're also advancing both the engineering and permitting of the White Mesa Mill Phase 2 expansion. It also means continuing our low-cost uranium production while progressing permitting and development of our uranium pipeline to support future production. We will approach these opportunities with discipline, matching development and capital commitments to the project readiness and economics.

The bigger picture is a company with 2 complementary priorities: first, building an integrated rare earth magnet materials business; and second, sustaining a strong uranium foundation. There is still work ahead and progress continues to depend on execution, government approvals and sound investment decisions. But our direction is clear. We intend to turn the capabilities we're assembling into operating business units that create substantial cash flow and long-term value for our shareholders. With that, I'd like to thank you for joining us today, and thank you for your interest in Energy Fuels.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Brian Lee with Goldman Sachs.

Brian Lee: Maybe just to start off, I know things are fluid and there's a lot of sort of regulatory approvals and different things that are pending to move forward on some of your projects and assets. When I look specifically at the Slide 5 in your presentation, I might have missed this, but it seems like a few things may have moved out to the right a little bit, Bahia from 2030 to 2031. Maybe just comment on kind of the latest thoughts around this flow sheet in terms of ramping up different capacity across your various segments. I know Donald sounds like it's kind of back on track to be end of this year after a few slippages this year.

But just in general, kind of what you're seeing on the broader flow sheet here in terms of capacity time line?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Thanks, Brian. Thanks for the questions, and good to talk to you. Look, Donald, I think, is pretty much in line. We hope to make the FID, like I said, before the end of the year. I think that's going to be really important to get that into construction, and we hope that will kick off fairly quickly after FID, 22-month or so construction time line to bring that into production. On the Vara Mada front, we remain subject to government approvals and government work there. And so there is a little bit more uncertainty around timing of Vara Mada.

But I think we are making good progress there, and we can talk to that if that would make more sense later. But I do think that we are on track to a large extent for most of these. Phase 1B and 1C, we're probably looking at early '28 for that work. Phase 2, I think we're very much on track for getting the -- getting our environmental approval that's being done through the State of Utah and very much on track for those approvals sometime next year, and then we'll make an FID post that. The AMP, the timing of the AMP is really going to be dependent on market conditions.

So what we're looking at there is we're expanding the KMP, the Korean Metals Plant. That work is going very well. We're going to have capacity of around 3,600 tonnes with the addition of our new strip caster there. So we've got good capacity, and then it will really be driven when we build the ASM facility or the AMP facility, the American Metals Plant, depending on market conditions, and we're projecting that sometime in 2029 for right now. So there is a little bit of fluidity on areas that we don't have control over. But where we do have control, I think we're on track with what we're projecting to be done.

Brian Lee: Okay. That's helpful. Maybe a follow-up just on Donald. Assuming you reach FID by the end of this calendar year there, how quickly do you start to see some operational impact from that asset? Like what are the milestones that are still needed to be achieved there? And then I guess, how do we see it show up in your operations and P&L? Would there be something that we actually start to see in 2027? Or is this all 2028 and beyond?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. For Donald, it's really 2028 and beyond. Like I said, the construction time line is about 22 months for Donald. So assuming we kick that off late this year, early next year, you're then looking at late 2028 for first production. And that will get fed to the White Mesa Mill. And so we'll start seeing that in late '28.

Brian Lee: Okay. Great. Maybe last one for me, and I'll pass it on. I know there's only so much you can comment on in terms of VAC and the issue with the offtake customer. Can you just maybe zooming out, talk to the ability for that Sumter capacity to be allocated elsewhere? What are sort of the fallback plans in terms of being able to secure more offtake and commercial traction on that 2,000 tonnes of capacity? And in what time frame maybe?

Ross Bhappu: Sure. So again, I want to reiterate, we were aware of this customer dispute before we announced the transaction. It was built into our economics. It was built into our cash flow assumptions and our EBITDA assumptions. So nothing's changed as a result of that customer dispute, and that was already built into our economics. What I would say is there is capacity available. We are utilizing the Sumter facility for a few contracts right now, but there is additional capacity available if that contract does, in fact, end. So we do have capacity. We are in discussion with a number of different groups to fill that capacity.

There's a lot of interest out there, and we anticipate we'll fill that hopefully fairly quickly. So -- but again, I want to reiterate that there's been no change in our minds with what was put out in the press about that contract.

Operator: Your next question comes from Nick Giles of B. Riley Securities.

Nick Giles: It was nice to see KMP contributing its first alloy sales. Ross, you mentioned the expansion to 3,600 tonnes. I was just wondering if you could walk us through kind of the economics of that plant, how we should kind of think about the margin profile there? And ultimately, ahead of White Mesa oxide becoming available in 2028, how you're looking at sourcing oxide to fill any of the expanded capacity and just how that supply is structured?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Thanks, Nick, and good talking to you. So yes, ASM has been on this kind of continued growth path. We -- over the course of the past year, the company and the project, they've installed 8 new furnaces. I think a key milestone was getting this new strip caster. And that strip caster, as I mentioned on the call -- on the notes on the presentation, is being installed as we speak. And that's a major piece of equipment that allows us to go from 1,200 or 1,300 tonnes per year to 3,600 tonnes per year.

Of course, the one issue that ASM always has and will continue to have is, as you point out, sourcing the raw materials and ensuring they have adequate feed to grow that business. Part of the strategy, this whole integration strategy is removing the reliance on external third parties to source that raw material feed. And that's where our mines in the White Mesa Mill come into play. So keep in mind that the mines will feed ore to the mill, the mill will produce oxides. Those oxides will then be sent to the Korean Metals Plant where they're converted to metals and alloys. And then those metals and alloys get sent to VAC where they'll get converted into magnets.

So ASM has a number of contracts with existing magnet manufacturers. As it ramps up, the economics of the plant will continue to improve. And those margins will continue to hopefully improve as capacity ramps up and the operating costs go down. That's about as much as I can say on the profitability of the plant. It is a facility that effectively operates on a tolling business today, but it will transition now to a key part of our value addition stream and a key part of our process. So that whole vertical integration, this is a pinch point that we think is very important.

Nick Giles: No, I appreciate those comments, Ross. And yes, I think when White Mesa comes online, it's clear the value of that asset. I guess just to clarify, we shouldn't think of that operation as one that could really generate positive free cash flow ahead of White Mesa sourcing. Is that a fair assumption as we try and model that asset?

Ross Bhappu: I think it's fair to say that, that asset will generate some positive cash flow and EBITDA, but it won't be a massive generator until we get White Mesa ramped up and fully operational.

Ross Bhappu: Sorry, Nick, just to be clear, I mean, I think that would come from Phase 1B and 1C where we could see meaningful supplies being provided to the KMP.

Nick Giles: Correct, right. Right. Okay. My second question was really just around funding and specifically on the OSC loan. I was hoping you could give us some more color on kind of where the process stands in finalizing that capital. Is there anything that Energy Fuels still needs to provide from a due diligence perspective? I appreciate any update.

Ross Bhappu: Yes. It's a good question because it's very timely. We're right in the middle of due diligence with the OSC and the OSC has 3 outside firms that they're using to conduct due diligence. I have to say it's very, very thorough. And in fact, we have a due diligence on site at some of the operations today as we speak. So that due diligence is continuing. We anticipate moving to final documentation, hopefully, over the next couple of months. And I don't have a specific timing on closing, but we're hoping kind of by year-end, we'll have good clarity on that and hopefully, early in the new year being able to draw on that funding.

But it's still -- they still are in the middle of their due diligence, and it's very active.

Heiko Ihle: That's fair. And then just a little bit on the site, the mill maintenance. Ross Bhappu: Yes. So our plan right now, the mill has been shut down. As you recall, the mill will outrun the mines. #3284. IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

The search tool offers summaries and verifiable source links

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

IEEE recently released the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite, built on the full text of millions of peer-reviewed publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library. The library offers full-text access to IEEE standards, journals, magazines, conference proceedings, and more.

Researchers who use the AI suite to search the digital library receive answers grounded in verified scientific results, ensuring a high level of accuracy and trust.

Powered by a proprietary AI system optimized for STEM literature, the suite introduces powerful, intelligent features within the digital library. The suite enables users to seamlessly search and discover articles to accelerate their comprehension of complex technical papers.

The system surfaces deep insights, replacing the typical keyword queries with natural, conversational research workflows.

As AI tools become more common in conducting research, IEEE collaborated to build the suite around a simple principle: Answers should be trustworthy, not just fast, says W. Clem Karl, vice president, IEEE Publication Services and Products.

“AI can be a highly effective and beneficial tool that can help researchers accelerate discovery, enhance decision-making, and surface new connections,” Karl says. “However, many AI engines present a great risk of hallucinating answers or introducing bias into otherwise credible research. With this in mind, IEEE has taken a responsible approach in our AI strategy by developing concrete safeguards to ensure our solution is rigorously grounded in scientific evidence that users can trust.

“As stewards of the scholarly record, we held the new AI engine to the same standards as the peer-reviewed research we publish: A researcher shouldn’t have to trust an answer; they should be able to verify the work behind it.”

The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite was developed in close collaboration with global scientific and library communities.

The development process began with research into user needs and the challenges associated with existing AI research assistants. More than 3,000 testers—including engineers, scientists, and library information professionals—provided feedback to refine the AI engine and support research workflows.

To mitigate the risk of AI hallucinations, the search-retrieval process is limited to querying the millions of IEEE peer-reviewed full-text documents, alongside an expertly curated dataset of STEM metadata. If the AI tool is unable to find relevant scientific content within the defined dataset, it is designed to inform the user rather than generate fabricated answers.

“IEEE is committed to providing the technical community with a highly precise and reliable research experience,” says Steven Heffner, IEEE’s chief publication officer and managing director of IEEE Publications. “The IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite offers something unique in that it is the only AI research assistant that leverages both the full-text and metadata of IEEE’s peer-reviewed content, rather than abstracts alone.

“The difference is significant: Our internal testing showed a threefold increase in result quality and accuracy across every key metric. These results underscore how critical full-text grounding is for technical research.”

For more information about features and coverage, or to request a demo for your organization, visit the IEEE Xplore AI Research Suite website.

Claire Olini is the senior manager for IEEE Corporate and Strategic Product Launch and Engagement.

Michael Spada is director of IEEE Product Launch and Engagement Strategy.

#3283. tvOS 27.2 adds new Apple TV 4K setting that’s an instant favorite

tvOS 27.2 launched last week as the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it includes a new setting I’m a big fan of: Shuffle for screen savers.

Screen savers have been one of the best Apple TV features since tvOS first launched in 2015. Largely that’s due to the gorgeous aerials captured around the world (and even from space).

Aerials are still my favorite type of Apple TV screen saver, but tvOS has steadily added other categories worth checking out too.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

The second and third options tap into your Apple Photos library and introduce the joy of seeing your favorite memories pop up on the big screen. Snoopy screen savers feature the beloved Peanuts character in a variety of entertaining scenes.

All of these screen saver options are great. But until tvOS 27.2, you had to select just one category and that’s all you’d ever see.

Now with tvOS 27.2, Apple has introduced a ‘Shuffle’ option that randomly cycles through screen savers from across all four categories.

It’s a welcome new setting, long overdue but I’ve been enjoying it a lot. The ability to be surprised by more different screen savers may sound like a small thing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to the Apple TV 4K experience.

Have you tried the new Shuffle setting for screen savers in tvOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

#3282. Zipline raises $1.5bn at $21.5bn valuation as Walmart adds 300 drone sites

Zipline’s valuation has nearly tripled since January. Uber is targeting a million drone deliveries a day with it by 2029, and Zipline plans to build more drones in the US.

A Zipline long-range drone drops a package by parachute.

Zipline has raised $1.5bn at a $21.5bn valuation, the drone delivery company announced on Thursday. Paradigm, WCM Investment Management and Layer Global led the round. Valor Equity Partners, Fidelity, Uber, Tiger Global, J.P. Morgan, ARK Invest and Salesforce Ventures also invested.

On the same day, Walmart agreed to add 300 Zipline drone delivery sites in the US under a new multi-year deal. The two companies run 21 sites in Texas and Arkansas today, Bloomberg reported.

The valuation is almost three times the one Zipline reached in January, when it raised more than $600m. Bloomberg and Reuters put that earlier figure at $7.6bn, while The Wall Street Journal put it at $7.85bn.

Founder and chief executive Keller Cliffton told Bloomberg Television that demand had surprised both companies.

“I think both we and they have been quite startled by the level of customer demand.” Keller Cliffton, founder and CEO, Zipline

Zipline said it will use the money to expand its US manufacturing and hire more staff as it builds a nationwide drone delivery network. Its factory near San Francisco International Airport can make up to 20,000 aircraft a year, according to Bloomberg.

Uber, which partnered with Zipline in August, is targeting 1m drone deliveries a day with the company by 2029, Zipline said. Zipline made more than 1m deliveries in the Dallas-Fort Worth area this year. Its median order in October arrived 19 minutes after checkout, against 30 minutes or more for ground delivery, the company said.

A group of its longest-standing restaurant partners saw delivery sales rise 26% between March and October. Zipline orders made up 80% of that increase, according to the company.

Cliffton co-founded Zipline in 2014. It began by flying blood to hospitals in Rwanda. Its African business now generates positive cash flow, Cliffton told Bloomberg. The company says it has flown 150m commercial autonomous miles without a safety incident.

It runs two drones. A long-range aircraft drops packages by parachute, and a quieter short-range drone lowers home deliveries on a tether. In the US, Zipline flies in Texas, Arkansas and Ohio. It plans to launch in Arizona soon, Kelly Cloonan reported for The Wall Street Journal.

Cliffton told the Journal that the national build-out would be hard.

“We have experience doing that, but still, this is a different scale and it’s going to be hard.” Keller Cliffton, Zipline

Regulatory approvals and community concerns over noise and safety still stand in the way of wider drone delivery, Reuters reported. Walmart also works with Alphabet’s Wing. Amazon is growing its drone service to about 500 US locations. DoorDash is building its own drones, and Ireland’s Manna is building a US factory.

#3281. Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Personal Finance feature

Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

“Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself,” Anthropic says. “With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Similar to ChatGPT’s finances feature, Claude’s new capabilities essentially give you a way to use chat as a way to make sense of your finance data. It can also present data in dashboards, calendars, and more.

Given the importance of security, here’s what Anthropic has to say regarding the new finance feature and Claude:

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That’s where you agree to its terms and approve Claude’s read-only access, so Claude doesn’t ask for or see your bank password.

#3280. I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing

Benjamin Skuse set out to test whether AI-generated research could pass for the real thing.

Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.

According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.

Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.

“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”

Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.Round 1: Creating the ForgeryTo give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.Luigi AvantaggiatoI assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI Jorge Cuadel CalleI took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.ROUND 2: FARS1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. See the AI-Generated Papers Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.

The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?

Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.

To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.

Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.

I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.

My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.

I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.

At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.

What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”

Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.

I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.

1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.

2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.

3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”

4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.

5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.

2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.

3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.

4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.

5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.

→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.

Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?

As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!

In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”

Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.

On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.

These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.

It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.

Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.

Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.

Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.

There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.

Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.

Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”

My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?

Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.

What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?

Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.

The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”

FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)

Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.

FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.

Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.

With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.

At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.

Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.

“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.

In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.

Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.

“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”

Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?

In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”

Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”

In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”

To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”

Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.

Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.

Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.

Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.

Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Benjamin Skuse is a professional freelance writer of all things science and technology. Previously, he earned a Ph.D. in applied mathematics from the University of Edinburgh and an M.Sc. in science communication from the University of the West of England. His work has appeared in New Scientist, WIRED, Physics World, Sky & Telescope, Photonics Focus, and many more.
