#3254. Omar Hamdi says AI will test whether PR firms can really scale

Pathos chief Omar Hamdi argues that AI should make PR more efficient, measurable and useful to growth companies, rather than replace human judgement.

Omar Hamdi, founder and CEO of Pathos Communications, right, on a panel at Press Gazette’s Media Strategy Network USA in New York in March 2026.

City A.M. reported on 6 October that the share of UK firms spending on public relations and management consultants fell to 4.2% in September, even as overall business spending rose 3.1% year on year and spending on AI services increased rapidly.

For Omar Hamdi, chief executive of London-listed Pathos Communications plc, those figures are less a death notice for PR than a sharper test of its economics.

The question suggested by those figures is not only whether companies will cut agency budgets as AI tools spread. It is whether agencies can use technology to deliver more useful work, more consistently, at a price and margin that make sense.

Hamdi’s answer, by his account, is to build a PR company where software takes on more of the preparation, targeting and business development, while people still handle the relationships and judgement that matter when a company is trying to be understood.

Pathos’s recent numbers give that argument a public company frame. Investegate published Pathos’s results for the six months ended 30 June 2026 on 9 September, reporting 14% revenue growth, 36% adjusted EBITDA growth, an 80% rise in customer cash receipts and reoccurring customers accounting for 36% of revenue, compared with 16% a year earlier.

The same announcement said Pressella, its AI virtual publicist, and PathosMind remained on track for general availability in the first half of 2027.

Proactive Investors reported on the same day that Pathos’s first-half adjusted EBITDA rose as higher revenue, improved operating leverage and lower bad debt charges fed through to profitability. That is the operational point Hamdi keeps returning to. He says the firm’s technology is helping with lead generation, lead nurturing and onboarding, while repeat and reoccurring customer relationships are becoming a larger part of the business.

The practical change, as Hamdi describes it, starts before a prospect has spoken to anyone at Pathos. The technology analyses news, shares potential hooks and article ideas, and prepares materials for the human conversation that follows. By the time a meeting takes place, he says the team can have article drafts, business cases and current news hooks ready.

In delivery, he says Pathos is using algorithmic matching between client stories and publishers to improve the chances that content succeeds.

That matters because the addressable market Hamdi is thinking about is not a small pool of blue-chip communications departments. He points to a global market of 400 million SMEs.

In his telling, the technology is intended to make a serious PR experience available to companies that may not have had the time, budget or confidence to hire a conventional agency.

Prospects sometimes respond to outreach, he says, as if Pathos is already doing part of the publicist’s job. One reaction he recalls is: “I feel like you’re already my PR firm.”

The aim is not simply more automated content. Hamdi’s emphasis is on preparation that changes the quality of the first human interaction. He says clients felt they were getting the same experience they would receive if a highly qualified PR person with decades of experience had spent a day working with them, and were getting that experience “before they’d even met with us for the first time.”

There is also an internal productivity argument. Hamdi says the technology affects how the team works, not only how prospects are contacted.

“It just makes their job much more efficient, much more lubricated, the velocity of the business has improved,” he says. The efficiency of Pathos’s business development, he adds, is higher than it has ever been.

For business readers, the more interesting claim is not that AI can write faster. It is that what was originally a services company may be able to grow by becoming a technology company with a service layer. Hamdi says Pathos is adding larger and stronger publishers to its platform, which can support better margins with those publishers. “We’re getting more efficient as we scale,” he says.

Yahoo Finance reported on 15 October that Hamdi discussed rising repeat and reoccurring revenue, Pathos’s aim of building a sustainable, profitable listed business, and the planned first half 2027 launch of its AI-powered virtual publicist.

The broader bet is still to be tested as Pressella and PathosMind move toward wider availability. But the direction is clear enough. In Hamdi’s view, PR’s future belongs less to firms selling hours and more to operators that can use technology to scale judgement, preparation and relevance, without stripping out the human work that gives PR its value.

#3253. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

#3250. Meta adds real-time voice chat and animated avatars to its Muse app

Meta adds real-time voice chat and animated avatars to its Muse app

Meta has added live voice conversations to Muse, its personal AI agent, so users can talk to it instead of typing. The update also gives Muse an animated avatar that reacts as the conversation goes on.

The feature is available now in the Muse app on phones, the web and Mac, but only in the US for the moment. Users start a call by tapping the phone icon in the top-right corner of the app.

During a call, users can interrupt Muse at any point, and it answers straight away. Muse can also keep working on tasks in the background while the conversation continues, for example, while the user is out on a walk.

Alongside the voice, the avatar shows facial expressions and gestures that match the tone of the conversation. It also reacts while the user is still speaking.

Users can choose how much of it they see. They can talk with voice only, keep the avatar next to the conversation, or open it full screen. There are also hundreds of voices with different personalities, and users can switch between them at any time.

At Connect, Meta also said users would be able to shape a voice by describing it, for example by asking for a different speed or accent.

Meta suggests using the feature to brainstorm ideas, plan a trip or practise for a job interview or a presentation.

The avatars run on Muse Realtime Avatar, a model built by Meta Superintelligence Labs, the company’s main AI unit. Meta first showed the technology at its Connect conference in September.

In tests run by Meta’s own raters, people preferred its avatars to those of rivals Runway and HeyGen, the company said. However, Meta has also said that not all of its demonstrations reflect the avatars available in the app.

Muse itself launched in September as Meta’s answer to AI agents such as ChatGPT. It runs on the Muse Spark family of models, which Meta introduced in April, and it can already shop with retailers, send emails, and control apps on a Mac.

The launch is part of Meta’s heavy spending on AI, which includes its Hyperion data centre in Louisiana.

Voice conversations will come next to Meta’s AI glasses and to Muse Charm, a small clip-on device the company showed at Connect. Meta has not yet given a date for either.

#3249. When Electric Cars Were for Women

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

However, that didn't last, as a broad sell-off of tech stocks took place today in the wake of U.S. midterm election results.

The Democratic Party gained control of Congress, raising worries that incoming Democratic leadership could demand tighter AI regulations and put a hold on data center construction projects key to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. This could result in a major impact to Amazon's AWS business just as the company is spending substantial sums to expand its AI infrastructure.

At the same time, Wall Street is concerned about the e-commerce giant's AI costs. Last week, Amazon's third-quarter earnings report missed revenue estimates while the company's capital expenditures continued to rise, resulting in negative Q3 free cash flow (FCF) of $42.4 billion compared to positive FCF of $14.8 billion in the previous year.

In a macroeconomic environment of rising interest rates, which makes borrowing to fund an AI buildout more expensive, and persistent inflation likely to impact consumer spending and Amazon's sales, the company is facing a challenging time right now. But over the long run, its AI investments could position it for success. Management forecasted AWS revenue to grow by 40% year over year in 2027 and 2028 as well, thanks to strong demand for its AI offerings.

#3246. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3245. Instagram launches free Edits video editor for Mac with 4K exports

Instagram announced on Thursday that it is bringing Edits, its short-form video editing app, to desktop on Mac.The app is free to download, but it works only on Macs with Apple Silicon chips, from the M1 onwards, and users need an Instagram account to sign in.

Instagram first launched Edits on phones in April 2025 as a rival to CapCut, the editing app owned by TikTok’s parent company, ByteDance. More than 50 million creators now use the mobile version, the company told Gulf News.

The Mac app looks similar to the mobile one, but it gives editors more room and more tools for complex projects.

These include a timeline with several tracks, keyframes for smooth transitions, audio waveforms, and colour wheels and curves for adjusting the look of a clip.

Users can also import their own fonts and colour presets, known as LUTs, and set their own keyboard shortcuts.

In addition, the app comes with Instagram’s library of licensed, royalty-free music, hundreds of effects and unlimited automatic captions.

Once a video is finished, creators can post it straight to Instagram from the Mac, with tags and location, instead of moving the file to their phone first. Alternatively, they can export it in vertical or horizontal formats, in up to 4K and without a watermark.

The desktop app also works with AI agents. By switching on the Model Context Protocol, a standard that lets AI assistants use other software, creators can ask an agent to handle parts of the editing for them.

Matthew Simari, who leads Edits, said users can connect the agent they prefer, including Meta’s own Muse assistant. For example, a creator could ask Muse for a rough cut and then finish the edit by hand.

Some features are still missing, however. Users cannot yet work on the same project on both their phone and their Mac, although saved audio and text styles from the mobile app already carry over.

There is also no version for Windows yet, and Instagram said it plans to update the Mac app every week.

#3244. CleanMyMac now helps you clean up Gmail and manage Chrome tabs

MacPaw today announced an expansion of CleanMyMac’s capabilities beyond the app’s traditional Mac maintenance and optimization tools. Here are the details.

CleanMyMac got two new features today, Email Cleanup and Browser Care, which are “designed to help users tackle digital clutter throughout their workday,” MacPaw explains.

Interestingly, both features focus on Google services, with Email Cleanup targeting Gmail and Browser Care designed specifically for Chrome.

Email Cleanup also helps users identify emails taking up storage space shared across Gmail, Google Drive, and Google Photos, allowing them to reclaim it once those messages are permanently deleted.

As for Browser Care, it “helps users reclaim Mac memory and stay focused by identifying Google Chrome tabs that consume valuable resources or create unnecessary clutter,” according to the company’s press release.

It works via a Chrome browser extension that connects directly to CleanMyMac, and lets users access “near real-time,” as MacPaw put it, “memory usage, pause resource-intensive tabs, find duplicates across browser windows and identify pages that have been left open for hours or days.”

In practice, MacPaw says, Browser Care makes it easier to identify which background tabs are affecting the Mac’s performance, helping users address slowdowns and reduce distractions.

MacPaw also emphasizes that Email Cleanup requires confirmation before making changes, while Browser Care only closes or suspends tabs when users choose to do so. The company adds that page content, titles, and browsing history remain stored locally on the Mac.

Both features are rolling out today to users with an active CleanMyMac subscription. To learn more about today’s announcement, follow this link.

#3243. Genesis Energy (GEL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Deepwater shortfalls and Shenandoah updates shaped the quarter's results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Genesis Energy, L.P. (GEL -5.81%) reported third-quarter results and addressed operational delays in the Gulf of Mexico. Management stated that results were impacted by lower-than-expected volumes from certain deepwater production facilities and a planned turnaround at Salamanca moved into the third quarter. The company continued its capital allocation strategy by reducing high-cost preferred units and maintaining no borrowings on its senior secured credit facility. Management indicated that while some production has shifted to later periods, the long-term outlook for offshore infrastructure remains supported by active drilling on dedicated leases.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Genesis Energy, L.P. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Dwayne Morley. Thank you. You may begin.

Dwayne Morley: Good morning, and welcome to the 2026 third quarter conference call for Genesis Energy. Genesis Energy has three business segments. The offshore pipeline transportation segment is engaged in providing the critical infrastructure to move oil produced from the long-lived, world-class reservoirs in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico to onshore refining centers. The marine transportation segment is engaged in the maritime transportation of primarily refined petroleum products. The onshore transportation and services segment is engaged in the transportation, handling, blending, storage, and supply of energy products, including crude oil and refined products, primarily around refining centers, as well as the processing of sour gas streams to remove sulfur at refining operations.

Genesis' operations are primarily located in the Gulf Coast states and the Gulf of Mexico. During this call, management may be making forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The law provides safe harbor protection to encourage companies to provide forward-looking information. Genesis intends to avail itself of those safe harbor provisions and directs you to its most recently filed and future filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We also encourage you to visit our website at genesisenergy.com, where a copy of the press release we issued this morning is located. The press release also presents a reconciliation of non-GAAP financial measures to the comparable GAAP financial measures.

At this time, I would like to introduce Grant Sims, CEO of Genesis Energy L.P. Mr. Sims is joined by Kristen Jesulaitis, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Legal Officer, Ryan Sims, President and Chief Commercial Officer, and Louie Nicol, Chief Accounting Officer. With that, I will now turn the call over to Grant.

Grant Sims: Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us today. As noted in our earnings release this morning, our third quarter results came in modestly ahead of where we thought we would be internally. In broad terms, the third quarter played out consistent with what we described in August, with the back half of the year being shaped by two things largely outside of our control: hurricane season and the timing of producer activity in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. The weather cooperated in the third quarter, as we had no weather-related disruptions during what is typically the most active part of hurricane season.

Unfortunately, the benefit we would have otherwise expected to see was partially offset by lower-than-anticipated volumes from certain production facilities which flow exclusively through our pipelines. While volumes from a couple of these deepwater facilities are expected to be lower than originally anticipated in the fourth quarter, and in all likelihood, last through the early part of 2027, it is important to remember we have visibility to at least four new high-impact wells that are scheduled to be completed and turned to production over the coming quarters.

Ultimately, none of these temporary impacts change the amount of oil in the ground, the acreage that is dedicated to our pipelines, or the fact that none of this incremental production requires any additional capital from Genesis. It simply becomes a discussion around timing and when, not if, we will move the volumes through our offshore infrastructure. In the Gulf, things can slide to the right, but rarely is there a total geophysical bust. If there is, lost volumes are virtually certain to be replaced by new discoveries that are developed in the same geographic neighborhood.

Elsewhere, our onshore transportation and services segments once again performed ahead of our expectations, and our marine transportation segment was generally in line with our expectations, despite our final blue water dry docking of the year unexpectedly extending into the third quarter. Both of these businesses are being supported by the same set of macro fundamentals: strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, shifting crude and product flows into and around the Gulf Coast, and in marine, a Jones Act market that is, if anything, getting [audio distortion] level of activity around our irreplaceable midstream infrastructure in the Gulf of America, as well as the macro fundamentals driving our other businesses. With that, let me turn quickly to the balance sheet.

Following the significant financing activities we completed in the first half of the year, there is very little new to report this quarter. We ended the quarter with no borrowings outstanding under our $900 million senior secured credit facility, approximately $41.5 million of unrestricted cash on hand, no debt maturities until 2029, and a bank-calculated leverage ratio of approximately 5.03x. In February, we issued $750 million of 6.75% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and used the proceeds to take out, in full, the higher-cost 7.75% notes due 2028, which pushed our nearest senior note maturity out to 2029. We also upsized and extended our revolving senior secured credit facility with our extremely supportive bank group.

Additionally, as a reminder, we entered this year with approximately $529 million of our Series A cumulative preferred outstanding, paying a current cash rate of 11.24%, clearly the most expensive current pay paper anywhere in our capital structure. In nine months, we have retired roughly 40% of it, taking the remaining face amount down to approximately $311 million. I would point out, had we paid down debt rather than retiring this very expensive security, our bank-calculated leverage ratio would have been closer to 4.7x. We think running a little higher leverage ratio in the near term to get rid of such high-cost security is in the best interest of everyone else in the capital structure.

We will continue to focus on right-sizing and optimizing our capital structure, and we expect to be able to drive future cash savings over the next several years from three places. We will focus on reducing debt in absolute terms, opportunistically refinancing our higher coupon senior unsecured notes with lower coupons and extended maturities as they become callable at more attractive premiums beginning in the first half of 2027, and redeeming the remaining approximately $311 million of the 11.24% Series A cumulative preferred still outstanding, all as we work towards our ultimate long-term leverage target of around 4x.

Consistent with the all-of-the-above approach to capital allocation that we have discussed, both prior to and since turning cash flow positive, our board of directors declared a quarterly distribution of $0.20 per common unit. That is unchanged from last quarter, but represents an increase of approximately 21% as compared to the third quarter of last year. We would otherwise expect to thoughtfully and prudently grow distributions to our common unit holders over time, all while preserving our financial flexibility to pursue attractive organic and inorganic opportunities as they may emerge in the future. With that, I will go into a little more detail on each of our business segments. Let me start with the offshore.

As I mentioned earlier, our offshore pipeline transportation segment operated without any weather-related downtime during the quarter. The offset was lower-than-anticipated volumes. Specifically, that included unplanned curtailments at a couple of our legacy connected fields, the continuing challenges from two of the initial wells at Shenandoah, and a planned turnaround at Salamanca that the operator moved forward from the fourth quarter into the third quarter. As we said last quarter, we do not believe any of these items have long-term negative implications for the ultimate recovery reserves already discovered and being developed.

In the operator's view, and we would concur, these impacts are transitory and simply result in timing differences for when those reserves are produced and when those barrels enter our pipeline for transportation to shore. In this pricing environment, the producers are clearly incented to figure it out. They do, however, tend to play the long game, accepting lower current production in order to maximize total ultimate recoveries from these world-class hydrocarbon reservoirs. Things can indeed shift to the right, but that's precisely why we have minimum volume commitments, or MVCs, in most of our new contracts. We are protected to the downside, even if it takes longer than expected for them to execute.

Owing to certain things, about which we are not in position to go into a lot of detail, Shenandoah operated at or slightly below the MVC level in the third quarter and is expected to do so until several new wells come on. A rig is on location drilling a second well at the Monument field, and both wells will be tied back to Shenandoah at the producer's expense.

It is now projected that production from the first well has slipped into early next year, but we would expect additional throughput from these two Monument wells to be in the range of 20-25 KBD, or thousand barrels a day of oil, reaching that level sometime in the first quarter of 2027. Excuse me. The rig will then return to Shenandoah and drill a fifth producing well, with initial production from it expected to be ±20 KBD. A subsea pumping system is scheduled to be installed in 2028, improving well performance and, most importantly, maximizing the ultimate reserves to be recovered from Shenandoah.

Beyond 2028, there are at least four, and possibly as many as eight additional locations at Shenandoah proper, possibly another location at Monument, two, maybe three locations at the Shenandoah South field, and as we understand it, there are already four additional exploratory prospects that have been identified within a 30 mi radius of the Shenandoah production facility. Suffice it to say, regardless of near-term challenges, we expect significant volumes to flow across the Shenandoah production facility and exclusively into our 100% owned SYNC pipeline and onto shore through our 64% owned CHOPS pipeline for decades and decades to come without requiring any additional capital from us.

At Salamanca, there are currently two rigs on location drilling wells to be completed and tied into the Salamanca facility, the production from which will flow through our 100% owned SEKCO lateral and onto shore through our 64% owned Poseidon pipeline. We expect both of these wells at Salamanca to come online early in 2027, which should move total production closer to the facility's design capacity of 60 KBD-70 KBD.

Harbour Energy, doing business in the U.S. as Louisiana Land Oil and Gas, has added a second rig to their Gulf of America program, and this activity at Salamanca, as well as expected additional activity there and at Buckskin, which also is transported exclusively through our facilities, is consistent with their stated goal of doubling their production out of the Gulf by the end of 2028. Elsewhere across our connected fields, the expansion of BP's Atlantis facility, which I mentioned last quarter, came online in July.

A new development well at one of our legacy connected hubs is expected to be turned to production during the fourth quarter, and multiple well intervention and remediation projects are scheduled before year-end that, if successful, could add meaningfully to the volumes moving across our infrastructure. Stepping back from the individual fields for a moment and focusing rather on the macro, there are 16 deepwater drilling units currently active in the Gulf of America, and nine of them are working on leases contractually dedicated to flow through our existing pipelines, even though we move just a third of the current production out of the Gulf.

Our pipelines are in the sweet spot for future activity, especially the rapidly developing Deep Wilcox or high-pressure, high-temperature geologic play, and yet we believe there is a lot of runway left in the more mature Miocene play in the central Gulf. There is no doubt the deepwater Gulf is a world-class basin. Our infrastructure is in the right place at the right time and is already paid for. Producer interest remains robust. Interestingly, every single one of the new nine-square-mile blocks leased by the federal government in the central Gulf in its most recent sale sits within tieback range or within a 30 mi radius of an existing production facility connected exclusively to our existing pipelines.

The resource underneath and around our dedicated acreage, both discovered and yet to be found, is vast. The pace at which it gets developed will be set by our producer customers, not by us. But whenever those barrels are produced, they will move to shore through our pipelines under existing or new life-of-lease dedications and without the need for any growth capital from us. This is exactly what has supported our offshore business for the last three decades, and we will continue to support it for decades and decades to come.

Turning to marine, our marine transportation segment performed in line with our expectations during the quarter, despite the dry docking of one of our larger offshore units that began in the second quarter and extended further into the third quarter than originally planned. There are no dry dockings for offshore vessels expected for the rest of this year, so the fleet is back at full capacity in the fourth quarter. We're experiencing, in essence, 100% utilization of available capacity, and negotiated spot rates for all classes of vessels are extremely robust, which we believe will ultimately allow term contracts to follow higher.

Demand continues to be supported by strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, and in particular, we are beginning to see the impact of increased volumes of Venezuelan crude being run at Gulf Coast refineries and the derivative effect that heavy crude is having on demand to move intermediate refined products from one location to another along the Gulf Coast and connected inland waterways. Our fleet of inland heater barges is specifically designed to transport exactly these heavy intermediate refined products, and we are well-positioned to benefit as that demand continues to develop. On the supply side, nothing has changed.

There is essentially no net new construction of comp tonnage, and we see very little on the horizon that could significantly affect this tight supply and demand balance for marine tonnage. Our onshore transportation services segment once again performed ahead of our expectations. We continue to see strong volumes through our Texas City terminal and associated pipeline systems, as well as through Raceland and South Louisiana, supported by increasing volumes offshore moving onshore. In addition, certain of the opportunistic marketing opportunities that arose last quarter continued into the third quarter.

We believe that we could possibly benefit from such opportunities in 2027 and perhaps beyond, as some of the dislocations caused by the Iranian situation, the required reinjection of barrels previously withdrawn from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, as well as the resumption of significant crude imports from Venezuela, take years to fully return to historic norms. We are not building a business plan around it, nor are we budgeting for it in future periods, but we will capture such opportunities as they present themselves. Our legacy sulfur services business performed slightly below our expectations as operational issues at our largest host refinery reduced the supply of sour gas available for our sodium hydrosulfide, or NaHS, production.

Much of that seems to be behind us, and we are currently seeing higher operating rates as well as additional sulfur removal requirements as our two largest host refineries start running more sour crudes. We also remain in active dialogue with multiple parties to diversify our host refinery locations and restore our supply flexibility to historical levels. Looking ahead, we believe the market opportunity for NaHS will increase in future periods. In a post-COVID world, we lost market share in South America to low-cost flake NaHS coming out of China.

More and more of our historical copper mining customers are starting to realize the apparent short-term cost savings simply are not worth the operational headaches they have encountered from their trials of the inferior Chinese flake product. Taken together, we are hopeful we will be able to recapture a meaningful portion of the NaHS segment margin that we have lost in prior years, but that we know is there, given our historical level of activity and financial performance from this market-leading business. As we look towards the remainder of the year, we will likely be near or even possibly below the low end of our original guidance for adjusted EBITDA for the year.

Having said that, I would reiterate that coming in at or below the low end of 2026 guidance has little to do with the underlying fundamentals and the ultimate cash flow generating capabilities of our businesses, especially in our largest segment. In any event, we will remain disciplined and focused on what we can control. Stepping back and keeping everything important in focus, 2026 has indeed turned out to be a transformational year for Genesis, just as we anticipated.

Our businesses, while not without third-party operational challenges relative to our and our producer customers' expectations at the beginning of the year, have performed well enough to allow us to make meaningful progress on right-sizing our balance sheet and reducing the ongoing cash cost to run our business. This has been a very solid year under almost any objective metric, and we are proud to have delivered it. The operational side has simply taken a little longer than we and our producer customers had reasonably expected. We believe in the long-term value of our franchises, and we intend to execute the next phase of right-sizing our balance sheet and go after those additional cash savings available to us.

Rather than focusing on what could have been this year, our attention is squarely on executing that plan, and we believe it represents a compelling setup to continue creating value for everyone in the capital structure. Finally, I would like to say that the management team and the board of directors remain steadfast in our commitment to building long-term value for all our stakeholders, regardless of where you are in the capital structure. We believe the decisions we are making reflect this commitment and our confidence in Genesis moving forward. I would once again like to recognize our entire workforce for their individual efforts and unwavering commitment to safe, reliable, and responsible operations.

I am extremely proud to be associated with each and every one of you. With that, I will turn it back to the moderator for any questions.

Elvira Scotto: Great. Thank you. On the marine segment, the margin was up year-over-year. Utilization is effectively, I think you said 100%. Can you provide any quantitative framing around that gap between the current negotiated spot rates where legacy term contracts are rolling off? What percent of your fleet reprices to spot or new term over the next 12 months?

Grant Sims: Yeah. I would say that certainly in the latter part of the quarter and continuing on into the early part of fourth quarter, we are seeing rates firm well over 10% on a spot basis, and in some cases even higher than that. We have on our inland fleet, I think we have basically only 10% of our inland fleet is contracted beyond December 31st. We think that a large portion of that is going to get recontracted at higher rates. So that's a good situation to be in. Probably half of our offshore fleet is also going to be repriced, we think, into a substantially higher market.

As we've mentioned before, there is robust demand for the American Phoenix, which comes off of long-term contract in the third quarter of 2027. We would fully expect after she finishes a 45-day dry dock for her to potentially reprice into a 15%+ to 20% higher value than what she's currently working for.

Elvira Scotto: Okay. Excuse me. That's great. I guess just really a long-term question, because it does sound like there's a lot of growth potential over the next several years. I think you mentioned there's nine of the 16 active deepwater Gulf rigs are working on leases dedicated to your systems, and two new rigs are expected to enter service over the next several years. Is there any incremental color on timing of those couple new rigs? Can you size the potential throughput uplift if and when all of those nine currently active rigs complete their current wells and those wells reach peak production? I'm just trying to understand, what is the real potential upside here?

Understanding that it could take a while.

Grant Sims: Yeah. I think there is one rig coming in, expected to come into the Gulf, I believe in 2029 and another in 2030. So, not going to have any near-term implications on that. As a general proposition, rigs that are deepwater drilling units, which are drilling today, can take 120± days to drill and complete a well. Most of these wells would be anticipated to have IPs in the 10,000-15,000 barrel a day range, and ultimate recoveries to ±25 million-30 million barrels per wellbore. So, you can do a little bit of arithmetic around that. Now, obviously, you do have some amount of decline from legacy fields and wells that have been previously drilled.

But it is certainly the level of activity, and our view is more than adequate to offset the decline. We are hopeful to see a net increase in total production, and we will give you a better idea of what 2027 looks like, as I said, when we have a discussion around the fourth quarter.

Elvira Scotto: Great. Thank you very much.

Operator: This now concludes our question and answer session. I would like to turn the floor back over to Mr. Sims for closing comments.

Grant Sims: Again, thanks everyone for listening in this morning, and we look forward to visiting with you in future periods. Thanks again. Bye-bye.

Wired headphones are having their moment. As we turn to more physical media and collect more vinyl and cassette tapes, we need to get our hands on the best ways of listening to them. Is streaming dying? Well, no, not by any means. But more and more people who have invested in physical media need a way to listen to their music.

Anyone you talk to who had a music collection in the '80s and early ‘90s will tell you the same thing — the Sony TPS-L2 Walkman and the MDR-3 changed the audio game. You could take your music with you anywhere and look pretty stylish while listening.

In line with the retro audio revival, thanks to a trend of digital fatigue, Sony has reimagined its iconic 1979 headphones with the release of the MDR-3R.

In looks, there’s not much that separates the headphones back then from the headphones now. They’ve had minor upgrades to make them suited to modern music listening, but side by side they look virtually identical.

The headphones are featherlight at just 1.3 ounces, making them the lightest headphones in the Sony lineup. They have a flexible headband adjuster, too, to get your ideal fit.

They have the same classic earpads that come in blue and orange, with both included with purchase of the headphones. The wire has been updated to have a USB-C input, making it compatible with modern devices. There are also in-line controls with a microphone, making them feel like modern wired headphones without compromising the overall look.

You’re likely wondering how these headphones might sound. Since they’re essentially a replica, not much has changed, but Sony says minor adjustments have been made to retain the classic sound and make the headphones suited to more modern music.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The MDR-3R headphones keep the classic analog warmth of the originals with a few tweaks. The 23mm driver is based on the 1979 version, but offers a wider frequency range, so the bass is more manageable for the cans.

I haven’t listened with these headphones as of yet, so I can’t speak from first-hand experience, but if they’re anything like the Gadhouse Wesley Headphones, we can expect crackly warmth with a nostalgic feel, but these retro headphones have 40mm dynamic drivers.

So, how much will these cans be setting you back? Well, they’re actually pretty affordable at $59. They can easily complement the NW-WM1AM3 or the NW-WM1ZM3, Sony’s new Walkman devices.

This is also cheaper than other retro-style headphones on the market, since the Gadhouse Wesley Headphones cost $89.

But the exciting headphones launch isn’t all that Sony has in store for us. Fully embracing the influence Max Mayfield has had on us over the last few years, the MDR-3R headphones are also launching in a Stranger Things edition.

This design has a black headband with the choice of black or red earpads in the box. These cost a little more at $79, and $20 may seem a little steep simply for a different colorway, but Stranger Things fans will love this ode to the show.

#3241. Report: Apple captured half of global smartphone revenue in Q3

According to a new report from Counterpoint Research, Apple just recorded its highest-ever global smartphone revenue for a third calendar quarter. Here are the details.

In a report released earlier this week, Counterpoint Research mapped out the global smartphone market’s performance during the third quarter, which saw Apple capture its highest-ever share of industry revenue for the period.

Samsung, which came in second, accounted for 19% of global smartphone revenue, followed by Xiaomi at 6%, OPPO at 5%, and vivo at 4%.

In another record, Counterpoint says Apple saw the iPhone average selling price (ASP) hit an all-time-high of $1,031, up 19% year-over-year.

Counterpoint’s Research Director Tarun Pathak explained that the iPhone 18 Pro series contributed to Apple’s ASP growth, despite launching toward the end of the third calendar quarter:

“Apple remained the most resilient major brand in Q3 2026, with shipments nearly flat YoY. Apple has the pricing power to absorb rising memory costs and pass them on to consumers with minimal impact on demand. At the same time, ASP growth was supported by higher launch prices for the iPhone 18 Pro series, the absence of the base iPhone 18 from the launch and price increases across older models in September. Together, these factors helped Apple deliver strong revenue growth in an otherwise challenging market.”

Finally, the report noted that while Samsung still led the market in shipment share, its lead over Apple narrowed slightly, with the companies accounting for 22% and 21% of global smartphone shipments, respectively.

#3240. IEEE Computer Society Chapter Offers Webinars With Industry Experts

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Attendees in Region 4 learn about AI, cybersecurity, and more

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and secretary of the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter.

To help engineers keep up with emerging technologies such as AI, cloud computing, and sustainable infrastructure, and learn how they can be applied in practice, the IEEE Computer Society’s Central Indiana Chapter recently launched its Tech Talk Series.

The live webinar series connects IEEE members, undergrad and graduate students, and engineering professionals from IEEE Region 4 with industry practitioners. The monthly sessions have covered AI governance and security, agentic systems, and related topics. The sessions featured speakers from Apple, software company Tavant, and cybersecurity concern Zscaler.

Upcoming sessions and registration details are available on the IEEE Region 4 virtual events calendar.

Rather than presenting on emerging technologies only at a conceptual level, speakers discussed the design decisions behind specific tools and systems, how the systems are structured, and implementation challenges. They also shared lessons learned from using the tools in their daily work.

Sessions also include technical walkthroughs and practical examples.

The live format allows attendees to discuss and compare their approaches when evaluating and implementing new technologies with those used by other organizations.

The organizers chose to make the series virtual so that chapter members and other attendees could participate in technical discussions with engineers from major technology companies and eliminate the need to travel.

For young professionals, the sessions connect what they’ve learned in a classroom with the realities of the workplace.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Attendees learn how practitioners approach projects such as system architecture, reliability, security, governance, and product delivery. For experienced professionals, the talks offer a forum to examine new ways of designing, securing, and operating software systems, and compare technical approaches. They can ask questions relevant to systems being evaluated or deployed within their organization.

The most recent webinar, Feeding and Fencing AI Agents: Engineering Governed Agentic Systems on Real-Time Data, featured Gajendra Babu Thokala, a senior engineering leader at Apple in Seattle.

The IEEE senior member explained how teams can move beyond adding isolated AI features to applications and instead build governed AI-agent systems that use real-time business data to complete multistep business workflows.

Another recent session, Building AI Native Products: A Playbook for Agentic Systems, explored how products built around AI agents differ from traditional software. It also covered how agentic systems can help users complete multistep tasks and workflows. IEEE Senior Member Sandeep Shivam, a product and technology leader at Tavant in Dallas, led the webinar.

Those two sessions illustrate the series’ purpose: helping participants understand what a technology can do and what is required to use it responsibly.

Future sessions are being planned on areas including enterprise AI, software reliability, and responsible AI usage. In addition to speakers from technology companies, the chapter also plans to invite speakers from startups, universities, and research organizations.

Upcoming sessions are expected to cover cloud platforms, enterprise integrations, and the responsible development of AI systems.

Technical programs such as the Tech Talk Series give professionals and students access to expertise, help create connections across career levels, and make important engineering discussions available to a broader community.

Undergraduate and graduate students are invited to participate to gain exposure to technical decision-making and challenges encountered in professional engineering environments.

Siva Rama Krishna Varma Bayyavarapu is an IEEE senior member and the secretary of the IEEE Computer Society Central Indiana Chapter. He is also the chair of the IEEE Central Indiana Student Activities Committee.
