#3223. ArcelorMittal (MT) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Tariff quotas and Ukraine charges shaped a quarter of sharp EBITDA gains.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

ArcelorMittal S.A. (MT -3.31%) focused on the structural improvement of its earnings capacity through the implementation of enhanced European trade measures and strategic growth investments in key markets. Management reported that the new tariff rate quota framework has successfully reduced import penetration, allowing the company to restart all its European blast furnaces and strengthen its domestic order book. The company is navigating temporary headwinds from elevated energy costs in Europe and weather-related disruptions in its mining operations while maintaining its 2026 capital expenditure guidance. ArcelorMittal stated that its strategic projects in India, Brazil, and Liberia are progressing to support higher earnings and cash generation as they reach full capacity in 2027.

Daniel Fairclough: Good afternoon, everyone. This is Daniel Fairclough from the ArcelorMittal Investor Relations team. Thank you for joining this call to discuss ArcelorMittal's performance and progress in the third quarter of 2026. Leading today's call will be our CFO, Mr. Genuino Christino. Before we begin, I would like to mention a few housekeeping items. As usual, we will not be going through the results presentation, which was published this morning on our website. However, I do want to draw your attention to the disclaimers on slide 24 of that presentation. Following some opening remarks from Genuino, we will move directly to the Q&A session.

If you'd like to ask a question, then please do press star one on your keypad to join the queue. With that, I will hand the call over to Genuino.

Genuino Christino: Thanks, Daniel. Welcome, everyone, and thanks for joining today's call. As usual, I will keep my remarks brief. Let me begin with safety, which remains our highest priority. We are now approaching the end of the second year of our safety transformation. Through disciplined execution of our safety roadmaps, we are seeing more consistent performance across the group. This is encouraging, and we remain firmly focused on our ambition of achieving zero fatalities and zero serious injuries as quickly as possible. Turning now to the business, I would like to focus on three key points. First, our results continue to demonstrate the structural improvements in margins. Third quarter EBITDA was $2 billion, up 34% year-on-year.

EBITDA per ton increased to $155, which is $44 higher than a year ago and well above historical averages. This demonstrates that our portfolio optimization and strategic execution are delivering results, and I believe there is significantly more to come. Importantly, these results do not yet reflect the full benefit of the new European trade framework, which is restoring sustainability to the European steel industry. Given the length of our order book, the increases in steel prices flow through to earnings with a lag. In addition, around 25% of our European flat product volumes remain under annual contracts that have yet to reset. This brings me to my second point.

As imports normalize, customers are increasingly looking to domestic supply, and we are responding. The TRQ framework provides the opportunity for recently idled capacity to restart, restoring employment and providing direct benefits to the local and regional economy. During the quarter, imports of flat steel products were approximately 50% lower than a year ago. As expected, our European flat product shipments were higher in the third quarter against the second quarter, which is counter to the normal seasonal pattern. As inventories normalize, we expect more of this reduction in imports to translate into higher domestic shipments. Our order book continues to strengthen, and we expect shipments growth to accelerate in the fourth quarter and show a double-digit year-on-year improvement.

This momentum is expected to continue to build into 2027. As customers shift back towards domestic steel supply, we will see higher, more sustainable capacity utilization. With Dąbrowa, Asturias, and Fos back in operation, all of our European blast furnaces are now running, and we are well-placed to serve our customers reliably and efficiently. Higher utilization should support a return to healthy and sustainable levels of profitability and returns on capital across the industry. My third and final point is that ArcelorMittal is exceptionally well-positioned to deliver higher earnings, stronger returns on capital, and continued value creation for shareholders. An increasingly regionalized steel market provides a stronger foundation for sustainable profitability throughout the cycle.

I have already talked about the significantly improved outlook for our business in Europe. Our business in India continues to perform well. We are ramping up our higher added value capacity, and the year to September represented a new shipment record. In North America, we are seeing positive momentum across our franchise. Better import protections are a common theme, and lean inventories alongside growing demand from data centers, energy, infrastructure investment creates a positive outlook for 2027. Against this improved backdrop, ArcelorMittal is well-positioned to succeed. Our scale, our leadership positions in key markets, and our strong track record of product and process innovation will continue to set us apart from the competition.

We are proud of the entrepreneurial culture, which promotes accountability and a relentless focus on continuous improvement. A more supportive industry structure gives us an even greater opportunity to convert these advantages into higher earnings and stronger returns. Over the past four years, we have invested consistently in high-return strategic growth projects that are increasing our earnings capacity. Importantly, many of these projects have not yet reached their full potential, providing a further source of earnings growth as we move into 2027 and beyond. The value created through these investments is further enhanced by our buyback program. This has been a powerful driver of shareholder value.

Given the positive outlook for free cash flow this year and beyond, I expect this to continue. With that, Daniel, I believe we can start the Q&A.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thank you, Genuino. We have quite a long list of questions to get through, but we will start with a question from Alain at Morgan Stanley. Hi, Alain. Please go ahead.

Speaker 2: Hi. Thank you for taking my question. Hi. Two questions from my side. I will start with the first one, which is the usual one, if you do not mind discussing the profit bridge into Q4, and specifically around Europe, where we are seeing many moving parts, including shipment growth, spot prices moving higher, but also elevated or sticky energy costs. Perhaps the same question applies to the other divisions as well, so if you do not mind starting with the bridge. Thank you.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah, sure. Thank you, Genuino. Thanks, Alain. Looking at the major components, the building blocks, the major themes into the fourth quarter, I think it is clear from Genuino's comments and the release that we expect higher volumes in the fourth quarter. That is a common theme, but in particular, we would expect that from Europe, where we have guided to flat volumes being accelerating in the fourth quarter and increasing year-on-year at a double-digit rate. Second component would be generally higher steel prices across the segments. Brazil, perhaps a slight exception to that, just given mix effects, so that is probably going to be a little bit more stable quarter-to-quarter. The third bucket or theme would be higher costs.

You talk about that in your question, the way you posed it, but I think everybody can appreciate the evolving cost dynamics, particularly in Europe, as energy prices have continued to evolve through the quarter. We will have to see how energy prices continue over the next six weeks or so. It is difficult to be specific there on the guidance, but that will clearly be a theme. The last component would be mining. We have guided to a stronger quarter to end the year from our mining segment, given the continued progress at Liberia and our expectation that should be operating at capacity in the fourth quarter. It should be a good quarter from a shipment standpoint.

Then, it is difficult to be specific on the iron ore and freight factors, but I am sure you can accommodate that in your expectations as they become apparent. Then I think just my final comment would be on free cash flow. If you look at our release, if you look at the presentation, we are expecting a good free cash flow performance in the fourth quarter, and that will be in substantial part driven by an expected seasonal release of working capital.

Speaker 2: Thank you, Daniel. Thank you. My second question is, if we stay with Europe into 2027, you talked about the annual contract resets. Do you mind reminding us how many tons will be up for repricing on 1st of January and how quickly this will feed through your ASP? In Europe as well, in your presentation, you talk quite extensively about the benefits of the TRQ framework, which hasn't fully yet fed through your profit and margins. What do you expect to see as we head into early 2027 that will drive the margin upside for your European division? Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Okay. Thank you, Alain. Let me take your second question. First of all, I think it's important to say that TRQ, Q3, of course, was the first quarter in which we could see the benefits of the new framework. We are, of course, very happy with what we have seen. As we were guiding at the time of quarter two, we see higher shipments and flat despite the seasonality, and despite the fact that we were going through a destock during the quarter. It's really working as initially designed, which should then allow us to bring back the capacity that I also talked about at the beginning in my opening remarks.

We will really see the full benefits of the new framework, of course, in 2027, Alain. Also what it does, and we believe it should really be extremely helpful, it allows the industry now to pass on higher costs, right? We are seeing now, we were in a positive trend in terms of recovering our margins. Of course, we were hit by higher energy costs. We are in the process of recovering that. When I look at the pricing guidelines that we have already for January, I'm sure you have seen it's already significantly higher than what you see at the moment coming from index. That's all very positive. We're going to be working through the destocking.

Our expectation is that destocking should largely end in Q4. When I look at the business and the moving parts, I think we can be very optimistic for 2027.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Genuino. Then just coming to your question on contracts, Alain. I think in our release in the presentation, you can see, and you already know it, that 25%, or approximately 25% of our flat volumes in Europe are annual contract. That is predominantly with the automotive customers, and the significant majority of those contracts follow the calendar year. So, a significant majority of that 25% of our flat volumes is set to reprice as we start 2027, which is another significant component of your positive bridge, I think, into the first quarter and for 2027 as a whole.

Speaker 2: Thank you. Thank you very much.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Alain. We will move now to take a question from Reinhardt at Bank of America. Hi, Reinhardt.

Reinhardt: Afternoon, Genuino and Daniel. Thank you very much for the time. Just want to ask about the European furnace restart so far. Can you give us an update on where exactly they are in their ramp-up process and when you think they are going to hit steady state production? I guess related to that, it would be good to get your thoughts on when you think there will be enough demand in Europe for you to actually start bringing some slabs in, perhaps.

Genuino Christino: Yeah, Reinhardt. Sure. First of all, we are bringing capacity as we see demand, right? I think that's number one, I would say. We are not bringing capacity unless, of course, we can see that in our order books. That's why we feel confident to bring back the capacity, because we are seeing order books strengthening. In terms of the ramp-ups, as you know, I mean, it's not easy to bring back capacity, especially when the furnaces have been idle for some time, which was clearly the case here. Poland, we are now up and running since the end of September. We have basically completed the ramp-up. The furnace is running well.

Fos, we are still going through the ramp-up phase. Not yet where we want it to be, but progressing there. In Spain, we are up and running. Two out of three furnaces are running well, and Fos is still in the process of ramp-up.

Reinhardt: Got it. That's clear. A comment on slabs, if you can?

Genuino Christino: Sorry, what was your question on the slabs, Reinhardt?

Reinhardt: When you expect demand to be sufficient in Europe for it to make sense for you to bring in slabs into the continent?

Genuino Christino: Well, I mean, look, I mean, this is something that, of course, remains a possibility for us. Our focus right now, Reinhardt, is to ramp up our capacity domestically, right? So that we can utilize our existing furnaces and tools that we have here. But of course, we have that flexibility. We know already what is the potential for higher volumes next year, just because of the TRQ and low imports that we expect to materialize. We're going to see the full benefits in 2027, right? But of course, we believe that we will have the capacity domestically to take care of that. But as a group, we have optionality, we have flexibility.

Reinhardt: That's very clear. Thank you. Maybe just one more question on developments into Q4. So, I mean, you've previously called out that some of this new capacity does have higher carbon costs associated with it. So, as you're building volumes into the fourth quarter, how should we think about improved fixed cost absorption and EBITDA per ton from that volume increase?

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Our message is the same, Reinhardt. Yes, as we bring back capacity, there will be more CO2 costs. But fixed costs, we shouldn't be really adding much in terms of fixed costs. So, profitability of this volume should be at least as par with the existing business, if not a little bit better.

Reinhardt: Very clear. Thank you very much, Genuino and Daniel.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Reinhardt. We'll move now to take a question from Tristan at BNP Paribas. Hi, Tristan. How are you?

Tristan: Yes. Hi. Thank you for taking my questions. I have two. First one is on Europe. One of your peer said that the shutdown of Ilva would be a game changer for the market. Do you share that view? Do you see a scenario where Southern European prices would trade at a premium to Northern prices? Does that mean ultimately that it could be upside risk to the market share gains you initially contemplated? That would be my first question.

Genuino Christino: Yeah, Tristan. Look, I mean, we all know in which levels ADI was running at, right? We all know. It was not running at very high levels. As a company, we feel we are in a good position here to service that market. As you know, we started Fos, the second furnace in Fos in the south, and we started also our furnace in Spain. It places us in a very good position to supply the market in south. Where prices finally settle in south, I mean, historically, as we know, south has always traded prices were always at a discount to north because of the more exposed to imports, which, as we know now, is being corrected by TRQ.

We'll see where prices finally settle. I wouldn't expect that to trade at a significant premium, but it will depend on trade and other aspects. But again, I think for us, it's a good opportunity to service that market from our facilities in the south.

Daniel Fairclough: Yeah. To round up that comment, I think as we look out there, I wouldn't say Ilva is going to have a significant impact. Just reinforcing Genuino's comment that they've been operating at very, very low levels. So the fact, if they drop down a little bit further, I don't think it's really going to change that supply-demand balance notably. So I wouldn't expect any significant or material impact on the market.

Tristan: All right. That's very clear. My second question is on North America. Could you discuss a little bit the strike impact in Canada and also what happened in Mexico? Is there anything structural at play, given it's been a couple quarters with some hiccups? How much of those, I mean, if you could quantify those one-offs and how much you expect to get back into Q4, that'd be great. Thank you.

Genuino Christino: Sure, Tristan. We had two events in North America. One was the strike in our longs division in Canada. That has been addressed. The facilities have been running since beginning of the quarter, so there shouldn't be any further impact from the strike. Back to normal levels. In Mexico, we had reliability issues with our DRI facility, which has also been resolved, addressed. I would expect us to be running at a normal capacity in quarter four, Tristan.

Tristan: And the negative impact, could you quantify it?

Genuino Christino: We are talking about in Q3, I mean, the losses, I would say in the range of 150kt.

Daniel Fairclough: Great. Thanks, Tristan. We'll move now to take a question from Ephrem at Citi. Hi, Ephrem. Please go ahead.

Ephrem: Thanks, Daniel. Two questions. I'll just take them in turn. First, I'm just trying to gauge how conservative your guidance for double-digit year-on-year growth in flat products, volume shipments in Europe is for Q4. Very rough math. I mean, you did about 6.5 million tons in total last year in Europe. 70% assume that is flat. A 10% implies somewhere around a 450,000 tons increase year on year for Q4 2026. If imports are coming down by 2.5 million-3 million tons per quarter, and you maintain your market share of about 30%, I mean, you should be expecting about 700,000 to 800,000 or 900,000 tons increase.

It's almost a 20% increase in shipments, unless volumes have gone down or you're losing market share. Would that be a right math, or please point me where I'm wrong on terms of the amount of volume increase in flats you could expect?

Genuino Christino: Well, I think you've got all the moving parts right. I think the only one that I would also point to you, as we discussed before as well, is we are still going through what we believe is the destock in Europe, which, as I said, should normalize now during the quarter in Q4, which then should, of course, help us as we start 2027. I think that's the only missing piece that I would point to you. Daniel, anything else here you want to highlight?

Daniel Fairclough: No, Genuino. Yeah, it's a good question, Ephrem, and thanks for putting it forward, because as Genuino says, you're picking up the moving parts there. Because inventories are really providing a cushion over the second half period as we transition into this new mechanism. We saw the reduction in imports in Q3. We're going to see, or we expect to see that similar reduction in imports in Q4. But because inventories are being consumed through that period, it's not fully translating yet into our shipments, into our volumes.

But as soon as those inventories are consumed, as soon as they're at normal levels, and as Genuino said in an earlier response, we expect that by the end of the year, then all of that will be translating into our shipments and our production. We're ready for that. We're primed for that. We're going to see progress and evidence of it in Q4, but that then, that momentum is going to continue. It's going to provide a good foundation for the bridge into Q1 and 2027 as a whole as well.

Ephrem: Thank you. Sorry, my second question is on India and Hazira. Obviously, now you're saying ramp up in, or start in 2027, which was obviously flagged a little bit earlier. But should we kind of realistically expect any shipments from the incremental, any new capacity in 2027, or is it really a 2028 story in terms of more volumes? Could you kind of give us a sense as to where we are in the completion of construction process and ramp-up process in terms of the incremental 6 million capacity there?

Genuino Christino: Yeah, sure. I can maybe comment on that. As you know, we have already commissioned the downstream, so the new cold mill, automotive lines for the finishing. We are testing now the new coke oven batteries. We are making good progress with now with the upstream, the furnaces. We do expect to see already in 2027 higher volumes coming from the project. Our expectation is that in the first half of 2027, we will start to see already some action there. We will, of course, provide you guys with some more guidance on that as part of our Q4 results. But we should definitely see already some improvements in 2027, especially in the second half.

Daniel Fairclough: Thanks, Ephrem. We are going to move now to take a question from Timna at Wells Fargo. Hi, Timna.

Timna: Yeah. Hey, good afternoon. I wanted to switch gears to the Americas, if I could, and beginning with Brazil. The investments you are making there are pretty notable. How do you get comfortable with the outlook there given smaller trade protections, the recent election, and at least one of your other competitors there was sounding a bit more cautious than you are? If you could elaborate on the Brazil strategy, please.

Genuino Christino: Daniel, to be honest, I could not hear well the question. Have you heard it?

Daniel Fairclough: Yes, I have. Perhaps I can start, Genuino, and I am sure you will complement. But it was basically, Timna was asking around the outlook for Brazil given the election results, what our plans are for investments there. Would we reconsider them given the election outcome, given the relative lack of trade protection, and noting that one of the competitors, I think, on the long side of things was giving a more somber outlook for the market.

Genuino Christino: Yeah. Okay. No, thank you. Great. Look, I mean, I think we have to differentiate now between longs and flat in Brazil. I mean, when we look at the flat business, we do believe that at least for steel, I mean, we have already good levels of trade protection. We have recently anti-dumping on cold roll, galvanized, painted, which is of course a significant part of what we produce locally. We have seen imports coming down to normal levels. They were quite high in 2025, coming down now to more normalized levels. We have more to come. We have anti-dumping now also coming on HRC against China.

We feel that the government has taken steps to support the business on the flat side. In longs, we also have some protection, maybe not as much as we would like to see, and we continue to engage with the government. And where you see us investing right now in Brazil is in the flat side of the business, with more downstream, which is because it is short. It is important exactly there. So, and we feel that it will make a lot of sense for us to convert exports into more domestic volumes. And that is exactly what we are trying to do.

Timna: Okay, thanks. Sorry if it was not clear. I was referring to a flat roll producer, but your results in Brazil were quite strong, so maybe a different perspective. Switching gears, if I could, to the North America market. You also have some repricing, I would assume there, so would like to hear on the repricing and the perhaps benefit from any lower CRU discounts we have been hearing about. #3222. AI's Workforce Gap And The Lessons We Keep Forgetting

Phillip Marangella, Chief Marketing and Product Officer, EdgeConneX.

Every revolution is a story about people, and the race to build digital and AI infrastructure is no different. Behind the headlines about chips and power are human questions: Who benefits, who feels left behind and who will build it?

The AI era is built on concrete and conduit, and there simply aren’t enough skilled hands to make it happen.

According to the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, construction faced a shortage of roughly 439,000 workers as of November 2025. Associated Builders and Contractors estimates the industry needs 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and another 456,000 in 2027, while the National Center for Construction Education and Research projects that about 41% of the workforce will retire by 2031.

Electrical systems alone account for 45% to 70% of a data center build’s cost, according to International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, and McKinsey estimates the country will need 130,000 additional electricians by 2030 to build data centers and new manufacturing facilities.

To meet AI demand, the data center industry has to grow the talent pool. Many potential beneficiaries do not know what data centers are or the careers they offer. The industry needs workers across more than 230 specialist roles, from construction trades and facilities technicians to engineers, controls specialists and network technicians. Some require a degree, but many call for a trade credential or equivalent hands-on experience.

Demand is growing faster than traditional education pipelines can produce skilled workers. In 2025, Google committed $10 million to the Electrical Training Alliance to help train more than 100,000 electricians and 30,000 new apprentices within five years.

The challenge is considerable, but not without precedent. In 1940, as skilled workers were drafted and war production surged, the War Manpower Commission created Training Within Industry, which broke complex jobs into teachable steps. By the end of the war, more than 1.6 million workers in 16,500 plants had been certified.

The lesson: Workforce gaps close when industry and educators treat training as critical infrastructure.

The second half of the people story is opportunity. In Northern Virginia, Northern Virginia Community College offers the state’s first accredited associate degree in data center operations. Microsoft partners with the college on scholarships and internships, and Amazon Web Services has teamed with Virginia’s community college system to expand similar programs statewide.

Virginia’s legislative watchdog, JLARC, found in 2024 that a single data center building puts roughly 1,500 workers on-site at construction peak, but sustains about 50 permanent jobs once running. Goldman Sachs Research reported that construction jobs tied to data center development have grown by 216,000 since 2022, and PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer found that workers with AI skills now earn a 62% wage premium.

History suggests that as technologies mature, new opportunities emerge. When ATMs spread across American banking, economist James Bessen documented in the IMF’s Finance & Development that fewer tellers were needed per branch, yet banks opened more branches and teller employment held steady as the role evolved.

AI and other technology shifts are predicted to create a net 78 million new jobs worldwide by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum, and LinkedIn’s 2026 Jobs on the Rise ranked AI engineer as the fastest-growing U.S. role, with tech and AI-related jobs among the top five.

Workers in these roles are key to AI’s benefits, but none of that happens without data centers, and data centers do not happen without skilled workers.

Then there are the people attending town halls to stop data center builds, and their concerns deserve to be understood rather than dismissed. A Gallup survey found seven in 10 Americans oppose constructing an AI data center in their local area. Shawn Patterson of the Annenberg Public Policy Center told Newsweek that opposition jumped from 49% to 61% between surveys. The Brookings Institution reports that local opposition blocked or delayed 75 projects worth $130 billion in early 2026.

Like the workforce challenge, opposition to new ways of working is not without precedent. Luddites protested automation in the 19th century, and Time warned of “The Automation Jobless” in 1961. The anxiety was not irrational; it eased when new livelihoods became visible and attainable.

The way through this fear is not a louder argument. It is a more inclusive, fact-based discussion that treats people closest to the build-out as neighbors, not obstacles. That means transparency, open training programs, verifiable community benefits and local hiring commitments that get kept.

No community ever learned to love infrastructure. People made peace with power lines, highways and factories when those things stopped being built near them and started being built with them. AI and digital infrastructure will earn its place the same way every transformative shift has: one neighbor and one kept promise at a time.

Workforce gaps close when we build fast, practical on-ramps like apprenticeships and community college programs. Creating pathways from classrooms to technology careers has been an EdgeConneX priority for years, including Hello World, which uses AI and VR in project-based computer science classes at the K-12 level. We are on track to reach more than 100,000 students across the U.S. by early 2027, with a goal of 1 million by 2030. That matters because students do not pursue fields they have never seen themselves in.

Positive momentum increases when local people can see benefits today and a brighter future ahead. Opposition softens not through better marketing, but through shared benefit, meaningful jobs locals can get and the promise of more time being human. The AI build-out will be won or lost not only in innovation, but in the meaningful building of human infrastructure.

#3221. Athenahealth patients can ask Claude about their medical records now

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The partnership could provide one of the nation’s largest AI companies with a bevy of personal medical data.

A major US healthcare technology provider just teamed up with Anthropic to connect patient health records with Claude.

Athenahealth, a healthcare technology provider serving over 20% of the US population, launched a Model Context Protocol (MCP) compatible server that connects to Anthropic’s Claude. The server, named AthenaPatient MCP, allows the AI model to gather information from health records and answer related questions. The process is secure, according to Athenahealth, and requires patients to sign in with their account credentials.

AthenaPatient MCP is available only to Claude Pro and Claude Max users, which cost $20 and $100 per month, respectively. Not all Athenahealth patients will have their data shared with Claude, and not all Claude Pro and Claude Max users must opt in. Users must give Claude their authenticated Athenahealth credentials, can choose which health information Claude can access, and can revoke access at any time, according to the press release.

Also: The wearable health boom is creating a data overload for doctors – what happens next

Once authorized, Claude takes patients’ information like lab results, vitals, medications, health conditions, immunizations, visit history, diagnostic reports, allergies, procedures, and care plans into account when answering questions.

The AI partnership does not provide medical advice, according to Sam Lambson, vice president of product management, data & ecosystem at Athenahealth, who responded to ZDNET in an email. It also should not replace a clinician’s professional judgment or medical advice. “Patients should contact a qualified healthcare professional with questions about diagnosis, treatment, or changes to their care,” Lambson said.

It appears that the AthenaPatient MCP tool is designed to help patients better understand the information provided by health professionals, rather than to give them medical advice. So, one may ask AthenaPatient MCP about their latest blood test results, such as “What was my most recent red blood cell count?” but users shouldn’t expect Claude to explain how an abnormally high or low count may affect them.

Athenahealth says that the agreement prohibits Anthropic from using data accessed through this connection to train its models or improve its products.

Partnerships between big tech and big healthcare aren’t new. In fact, the collaboration between Athenahealth and Anthropic follows a larger trend across the health tech industry. Earlier this year, Microsoft teamed up with Mayo Clinic to develop an AI model for healthcare; Boston Children’s Hospital forged a partnership with OpenAI to develop an enterprise AI system for use across research, clinical, and administrative teams, according to a press release.

Also: Before you buy a smartwatch or smart ring, consider what you’re giving up

A growing number of Americans are consulting AI for medical advice. A recent survey from Pew Research Center found that 34% of US adults have talked with a chatbot for medical advice. This partnership makes the process slightly more secure by authorizing patient account credentials before granting the model access to health records.

Health data is extremely valuable, and tech companies are increasingly interested in partnering with healthcare providers to access it. Much of the “AI could cure cancer” messaging we hear relies on these humongous companies obtaining enough health data to train their AI models and link disease data to patient data. This is not to say, however, that solving this complex issue is the motive behind the partnership between Athenahealth and Anthropic.

Also: Asking AI for medical advice? There’s a right and wrong way, one doctor explains

A more reasonable explanation for such a partnership is that an AI that can answer patient queries could eliminate some of the admin work doctors do between patient visits, like answering questions about test results, giving Athenahealth doctors some time back.

Will partnerships like Anthropic and Athenahealth’s improve patient outcomes? That remains to be seen, but a recent survey by Pew Research Center found that Americans aren’t that confident on the matter. The largest shares of respondents still preferred that a human oversee AI when it’s used in a clinical context.

#3219. These 7 iPhone Duo-Ready Apps Make the Most of Apple’s New Foldable Phone

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Several creative apps are ready to take advantage of the iPhone Duo's many display configurations, with more to come.

In addition to giving the iPhone line a new design, the iPhone Duo lets developers take advantage of several new modes to play with. But this early into the iPhone Duo’s general release, apps are still catching up to what Apple’s foldable phone can do.

The shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos. Some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s gotten an iPhone Duo (or it’s coming soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

#3218. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3216. From Pilots To Payoff: The Top IT Priorities Every Executive Should Accomplish Before Year-End

Scott Francis is Technology Evangelist at PFU America, Inc. and Ricoh Document Scanners.

​As the end of 2026 draws near, the central question for business leaders has shifted from asking whether their organization is adopting and deploying AI fast enough to assessing whether AI is performing as expected. With IT budget planning for 2027 well underway, organizations should use the waning months of this year as a reality check that will serve to separate organizations positioned to scale in 2027 from those still catching up.​

There’s no question that the demand for AI is skyrocketing. What is unclear is whether organizations are meeting the projected return on investment thus far. Gartner predicts AI spend will reach $2.59 trillion globally this year, a substantial 47% increase over 2025.​​

With the end of the year quickly approaching, there is an opportunity to take stock and refocus on overcoming challenges to achieving ROI and readjust where necessary. Rather than taking a scattershot approach to AI deployments, organizations should take a measured, strategic approach on where to apply AI; for example, using one workflow, establishing KPIs and then tracking those quarter-over-quarter before expanding to more departments or enterprise-wide.​

As the saying goes, “life moves fast.” And we’ve seen from technological advancements over the last few years that AI moves just as fast. Many companies are already in the planning phase of employing agentic AI, according to McKinsey’s report, with 40% of companies surveyed already scaling agents, up from 27% in 2025.

Despite the positive uptick in deployments, organizations should prioritize getting current AI deployments right, determining what’s hindering ROI and preparing for the next phase of digital transformation.

AI systems are only as trustworthy as the data foundation, which is a major reason why prioritizing data quality is imperative. Flawed data takes on a new meaning in the AI era because it has the potential to undermine the models built on it.

The “2026 State of Data Integrity and AI Readiness” survey of data and analytics leaders puts a spotlight on data quality challenges: 43% of respondents cite data readiness as the most significant barrier to AI alignment with business objectives. Creating proactive strategies to fix bad data, including data errors, redundancy and more, is still one of the most inexpensive approaches to protecting against downstream damage. This imperative step provides organizations with the confidence that their AI deployments will meet performance expectations and transform data into the dependable foundation that reliable, high-performing AI requires.

Before expanding AI deployments and introducing agents, executives should audit whether the underlying systems can actually support agentic workflows, including clean data pipelines, defined APIs and integration between the systems agents need to touch.

Preparing teams well before AI is rolled out across the organization is critical. Skipping this step can breed employee resentment and pushback and result in lowering morale.

Workplace tension is already a challenge, and for good reason. A WRITER study found that “92% of the C-suite are actively cultivating ‘AI elite’ employees, while 60% plan layoffs for non-adopters.” Business leaders should not view AI as a replacement for skilled personnel; it should be used to surface insights and recommendations, while consequential decisions, especially those affecting employees or customers, remain in human hands.

Training, communication and genuine feedback loops are what separate adoption from chaos, making change management well worth the investment. Reskilling and preserving the human element build trust and catch the blind spots LLMs can’t.

IT leaders should be aware that AI is not immune from volatility, and a backup plan is mandatory. One well-publicized example of AI disruption is Anthropic’s suspension of global access to Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5 following a U.S. government export control directive. Access was later restored under a modified compliance structure; however, business leaders should take this incident seriously and acknowledge that government-initiated suspension or access restriction can occur without advance notice. Business leaders can address regulatory instability by identifying which models and vendors they rely on and identifying fallback options before a suspension forces an unplanned migration.

There is also a growing regulatory divide between jurisdictions. The U.S. export rule’s workforce application means enterprises with frontier AI API integrations and global engineering teams may be exposed to compliance risk regardless of where their servers are located. Gartner projects more than a third of enterprises will run localized AI platforms by 2027, up from just 5% in 2025. For multinational firms, this means agentic AI strategy can no longer be a single global architecture; it will need to incorporate jurisdiction-based contingency planning.

​The gap between AI pilots and AI payoff won’t close on its own. The executives who make real progress before year-end will be the ones connecting these three priorities to long-term success to achieve business goals and ROI goals. I believe it’s imperative for business leaders to focus on the fundamentals this year before expanding AI projects and incorporating agents, treating their data quality, teams, economics and risk as interconnected.​

Operator: Welcome to Strategic Education's Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call. I will now turn the call over to Terese Wilke, Senior Director of Investor Relations for Strategic Education. Mrs. Wilke, please go ahead.

With us today are Karl McDonnell, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Daniel Jackson, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer. Following today's remarks, we will open the call for questions. Please note that this call may include forward-looking statements made pursuant to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. The statements are based on current expectations and are subject to a number of assumptions, uncertainties, and risks that Strategic Education has identified in today's press release that could cause actual results to differ materially.

Further information about these and other relevant uncertainties may be found in Strategic Education's most recent annual report on Form 10-K, the 10-Q to be filed, and other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as Strategic Education's future eight-Ks, 10-Qs, and 10-Ks. Copies of these filings and the full press release are available for viewing on our website at strategiceducation.com. Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Karl. Karl, please go ahead.

Karl McDonnell: Thank you, Terese, and good morning, everyone. Our third quarter results reflect continued strength in the parts of SEI where we have been investing for growth: Education Technology Services, our broad employer strategy, and our U.S. healthcare portfolio. The strength in these areas, however, was mostly offset in the third quarter by our Australia segment, where the environment has proved more challenging than we expected. This morning, I'll briefly review the quarter, then I'll walk through each of our segments. As I do, I'll discuss the opportunities behind our intent to make 2027 a year of increased growth investments.

As always, unless I note otherwise, my comments refer to adjusted results on a constant currency basis, and those results exclude the $134 million non-cash impairment of goodwill and intangible assets in Australia that we recorded this quarter, and which I will discuss with that segment. Third quarter revenue was $320 million, essentially flat with the prior year. We did hold operating expense growth to less than 1%, resulting in operating income of $50 million, a 2% decrease, and an operating margin of 15.7%, 30 basis points below the prior year. Earnings per share increased 4% to $1.69, reflecting a lower share count from share repurchases.

Given the strong demand across ETS, and given our desire to accelerate our product roadmap to serve that demand, our intent is to increase our growth investments in ETS in 2027. These investments will slightly reduce the ETS segment-level operating margin next year, but will also result in higher revenue growth in our current five-year plan, defend Sophia's market leadership position, and strengthen Workforce Edge's ability to sign new corporate clients. Turning now to U.S. Higher Education. Total U.S. Higher Education enrollment declined 1% to approximately 84,700 students, as growth in employer-affiliated enrollment was offset by lower unaffiliated enrollment. Revenue was essentially flat at $214 million, as higher revenue per student offset the enrollment decline.

Our productivity initiatives continued to hold operating expense growth to less than 1%, including continued investments in growth. Operating income was $22 million, a 4% decline, and an operating margin of approximately 10%. Student retention reached 89.2%, a new all-time high for U.S. Higher Education. Our healthcare portfolio continues to be the strongest source of growth in U.S. Higher Education. Healthcare enrollment grew 9% in the quarter and now represents 54% of total U.S. Higher Education enrollment, up from 49% a year ago, an increase of 500 basis points over the last year. Healthcare is also central to our broad employer strategy. Roughly 38% of our healthcare enrollment comes from employer partners, and employer-affiliated enrollment overall reached 35% of U.S.

Higher Education total enrollment, up 200 basis points from the prior year. We are now extending that portfolio into licensure track programs. Earlier this year, Capella enrolled the first cohort in its pre-licensure Bachelor of Science in Nursing program, and Strayer enrolled its first students in the new Associate of Applied Science in Radiologic Technology. Early demand for both programs has exceeded our initial assumptions. These two programs join Strayer's Licensed Practical Nurse diploma and Capella's expanded nurse practitioner portfolio, all aimed at the healthcare talent our employer partners increasingly need. To support that demand, we intend to also increase our growth investments in U.S. healthcare in 2027 with funding for new programs, clinical faculty, expanded clinical and instructional capacity.

This will allow programs like pre-licensure nursing and radiologic technology to grow at the pace their demand supports. Turning to Australia. Total enrollment declined 9% to approximately 17,100 students, and revenue declined 7% to AUD 64 million. The Australian team continued to manage costs well, with operating expenses down 4%, and operating income was AUD 10 million compared with AUD 12.5 million in the prior year, and an operating margin of approximately 16%. The decline is entirely a function of international enrollment. Over the course of this year, the Australian government restrictions on international students have become materially more severe than we anticipated.

New visa approvals for prospective students have slowed sharply, and in some months declining as much as 80% versus the prior year. In addition, the government has effectively closed the onshore transfer market by requiring international students already in Australia to obtain a new visa in order to change institutions. Given this environment, we have lowered our near-term growth expectations for the ANZ segment, which resulted in this quarter's $134 million non-cash impairment. Notwithstanding the headwinds on international enrollment, our domestic enrollment continues to fare well. Domestic new enrollment has grown every quarter this year, including 9% in each of the second and third quarters, and domestic students now represent close to 70% of new enrollment in Australia.

The quality of Torrens' academic experience remains strong and has shown significant improvement over the past year. We were pleased to see Torrens University's performance in the 2025 Quality Indicators for Learning and Teaching Student Experience Survey, the most comprehensive national survey of current higher education students in Australia. Torrens achieved widespread momentum across all undergraduate indicators, including a rise to sixth nationally for undergraduate teaching quality, up significantly from 19th the year before. At the postgraduate level, Torrens continues to lead at the top tier of Australian higher education, ranking in the top four nationwide for both skills development and peer engagement, alongside a seventh place ranking in postgraduate teaching quality.

This performance against national sector benchmarks reinforces Torrens' value proposition and supports student retention and long-term brand equity in industry-aligned education. The quality of Torrens' academic programs, combined with our own success in growing domestic enrollment, gives us confidence to increase our growth investments in Australia's domestic market in 2027. We are expanding our existing Adelaide campus and will launch several new health science programs, and we also plan to open a new campus in Perth in late 2027. Western Australia is the fastest-growing state in the country, with population growth 50% higher than the national average.

Greater Perth is projected to add more than a half a million residents over the next decade, and its economy is concentrated in the sectors where our new programs are focused, namely healthcare, engineering, construction, and defense. Perth will also position Torrens well for international recruitment from Asia when those constraints ease. Turning now to an update on our outlook versus our notional model. Given our current forecast for the balance of this year and the fact that the international enrollment environment in Australia deteriorated since the first half of the year, it appears unlikely our full-year results will fall inside of our notional outlook.

In terms of 2027, given that our forward revenue growth is mostly a product of current-year enrollment, we think the most likely outcome for consolidated revenue next year is to be flat with this year. We expect the cost of the growth investments that I have described this morning to be approximately $50 million in 2027. However, the productivity savings achieved this year will offset nearly half of that, such that year-over-year increase in operating expenses will be limited to just 2%.

Given that these incremental investments are targeted to support areas of proven strength at SEI, that is, our two high-growth, high-margin platform businesses, our U.S. healthcare portfolio, and our domestic market growth in Australia, we have a high degree of confidence in their ability to return the company to its notional growth rates in 2028 and beyond. Regarding capital allocation, in addition to our regular quarterly dividend, we repurchased approximately 347,000 shares during the quarter for a total of $28.5 million. We ended the quarter with $139 million of cash and marketable securities and no debt.

Finally, as always, I'd like to take this opportunity to thank all of my colleagues here at SEI for their ongoing commitment and support to our students and our corporate partners. With that, Victor, we'd be happy to take questions.

Operator: Thank you. To ask a question, you will need to press star 11 on your telephone and wait for your name to be announced. To withdraw your question, please press star 11 again. Please stand by. We'll compile the Q&A roster. One moment for our first question. Our first question will come from the line of Jeff Silber from BMO Capital Markets. Your line is open.

Jeff Silber: Thanks so much. Karl, really appreciate you giving us some insight into 2027. I was hoping I could just double-click on that a little bit. Is it possible to talk about the different segments? I say, overall, you think revenue most likely flat, but could we see growth in ETS offset by declines in the other two? From a margin perspective, where do you think you'd have the most impact in terms of declining margins potentially next year?

Karl McDonnell: I think we're absolutely going to have growth in ETS, Jeff. I suspect we'll have lower growth in U.S. Higher Education, driven by the strength of the healthcare portfolio that I just described. Overall, that'll be offset by the continuation of the restrictions in Australia, although we do expect that with the addition of the Perth campus, the expanded programs in Adelaide, launching several asynchronous online programs throughout Australia, we do expect that new student growth in Australia will be growing year-over-year in the back half of 2027.

Just given the headwinds that we've had, it's going to take a few quarters for that to translate into total enrollment growth, so I would expect that probably in the first part of 2028. From a margin standpoint, I would estimate that it could be in the range of 300 to 400 basis points at ETS, and a little less than that in U.S. Higher Education and Australia.

Jeff Silber: Okay, that's really helpful. I really appreciate that. Moving back to, I guess, the U.S., we had an elections earlier this week. I'm not asking you for your crystal ball, but given, guys, where you're located, you're probably closer to most in terms of what's going on and what potentially could go on. Any changes you're expecting with the changeover in Congress towards Democratic control?

Karl McDonnell: Well, I'd say that in the U.S., we have a high degree of confidence in sort of the regulatory and quality posture of both Strayer and Capella. We try to work constructively with any regulators or members of Congress or the administration, regardless of party affiliation, and we look forward to engaging with them once the new Congress is inaugurated in January.

Jeff Silber: Okay, fair enough. Thanks so much.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question will come from the line of Alex Paris from Barrington Research. Your line is open.

Alex Paris: Hi, guys. Thanks for taking my question. I too appreciate the granular detail by segment and the look at 2027. I just had a question on unaffiliated enrollment. Obviously, it was down 4%. That is actually an improvement from the second quarter by my math, when it was down 5.5%. But it has been down for eight consecutive quarters now, and you have consistently said you do anticipate returning to mid-single digits at some point, but it is not an area of focus. I get it. I am wondering, has there been an impact on the funnel from LLM, AI search, and so on? Could that be a contributing factor?

Karl McDonnell: Good morning, Alex. First of all, on unaffiliated enrollment, that's predominantly undergraduate business. It's an area that's important to us, but it's not one of our main strategic priorities in the way that healthcare is. You're right that the rate of decline moderated in the third quarter. We expect it to continue to moderate throughout 2027, perhaps even reaching break-even or growth by the end of 2027. In terms of LLM, it's certainly something that we're watching, but we've been focused on a quality of demand over quantity of demand for going on two years now. We don't peg rate of increase or decrease in any inquiry volume that we're getting as being most important.

We're looking at admission yield and sort of the acquisition cost to lifetime value, and both of those are near all-time highs. Obviously, we want to be relevant and favorably represented in any search medium that people are using, including LLMs, so we have a lot of people that are focused on it. But I can't say that we've really seen any adverse impact from it yet.

Alex Paris: What are you specifically doing to respond to the changes in the way students look at colleges and universities?

Karl McDonnell: It's a multi-function, multidisciplinary set of initiatives that we have. I don't really want to go into details on this call, but we do have a robust set of things that we're doing that we have a pretty high level of confidence will help position us well, not just in LLMs, but frankly, in any search medium that people may use.

Alex Paris: Obviously, it's important, but again, just to be clear, you've not really seen any material impact from the AEO as opposed to SEO on unaffiliated enrollment?

Karl McDonnell: Yeah, because, I mean, put yourself in our position, Alex. It would be next to impossible to ascribe any rate of change to LLM or any other single variable. We're happy with the demand that we're getting. In healthcare in particular, it's much stronger than what we expected. The growth of those new programs is far ahead of where we expected them to be, by as much as a year perhaps. But we're not ignoring it. We have people that are focused on it. We expect that over time, the evolution will become more apparent. I just would say it's very early, and we haven't been able to ascribe any changes to that specifically.

Alex Paris: Got you. My last question, quickly on ANZ. I appreciate you are controlling the controllables, campus expansions, new campuses, a focus on domestic. Is there any light at the end of the tunnel with regulatory? Obviously, this has been going on for a couple years now, and we thought that there'd be an improvement this year because of a lifting of the caps, but by slow rolling the visas, it's had an even more dramatic effect on international enrollment. Any additional color there would be great.

Karl McDonnell: I was a little surprised, frankly, that the transfer requirement to get a new visa was implemented. That was not something that we anticipated. It is what it is. Eventually, we're going to get to a new normal, a normalized rate of international enrollment. I think we're much closer to that as opposed to being further away from it.

If we continue to grow domestic growth in the high single digits as we're doing, or frankly, even in the low double digits when we add the additional capacity in Adelaide and Perth, eventually that's going to result in new student growth, which, as I said in my prepared remarks, I think could be in the latter half of next year, leading to total enrollment growth in the first part of 2028. Then if we get an easing of these restrictions, which some people in Australia think will happen over the coming several years, that will just be added sort of enrollment that we will get. We are not building a strategy around it.

We are accepting it for what it is and building all of our growth capital around the domestic market. Given, as I said, the strong performance of Torrens academically in the federal QILT survey, we think we are well-positioned to grow our domestic market share.

Alex Paris: Great. Appreciate the color. Thank you. I will get back in the queue.

Operator: Thank you. Once again, that is star 11 for questions, star 11. Our next question will come from the line of Jasper Bibb from Truist Securities. Your line is open.

Jasper Bibb: Hey. Good morning, everyone. Apologies if I missed it, but I guess I just wanted to understand how you're thinking about EBIT margin expansions with 2026 at this point. Daniel Jackson: Hey, Jasper. Yeah, it might be a bad connection. I am not sure I got the full question. I think it was 2026 EBIT margin. Was that your question?

Jasper Bibb: Yeah. I apologize. I am switching to speakerphone now. Hopefully, you can hear me better, but

Jasper Bibb: I just wanted to understand kind of 4Q expectations so we have the right jumping off point for kind of all the 2027 comments you gave earlier on the call.

Daniel Jackson: Hey, Jasper, you're talking about margin, right?

Jasper Bibb: Yeah, margin or, I mean, revenue if you have it.

Daniel Jackson: Well, we don't give revenue, forward-looking revenue input. We have commented on margin, as you know, relative to the notional model of 200 basis points of expansion. Jasper Bibb: Okay. I guess, could you just kind of frame what you are seeing in new starts in the U.S. and how that informs your expectations for next year?

Karl McDonnell: Sure. Well, as I said, healthcare is very strong, growing almost double digits, 9% in the last quarter. That is well over half of our enrollments now, so we are confident that is going to continue to grow, and I suspect the growth rate will increase given the strength of the new pre-licensure programs. As Alex Paris noted, and I confirmed, the decline is moderating. We think it will continue to moderate.

So, net of everything that we are seeing, I suspect that we are going to have net positive new student enrollment growth in 2027, and the division as a whole will sort of mean revert toward mid-single digits as we work our way through the year.

Jasper Bibb: Okay. No, that makes sense. Maybe last one for me, the subscriptions at Sophia Learning just slowed a little bit from the second quarter. Karl McDonnell: It is almost entirely a function of anniversarying that large corporate client that we have. If you excluded that corporate client, direct-to-consumer subscription growth is still close to 20% and growing, holding that growth rate. So it is really a function of the anniversarying of that one client that is quite large.

Jasper Bibb: Okay. Understood. Thanks for taking the questions.

Operator: Thank you. I'm not showing any further questions at this time. I'd like to turn back over to Karl McDonnell, CEO, for closing remarks.

Karl McDonnell: Thank you, everybody. We look forward to discussing our fourth quarter results with you in February.
