#3211. Disneyland Is Training a Class of AI Robot Interns

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

From Pixar robots to help you park your car to droids roaming Star Wars land, physical AI is popping up all over Disneyland.

If you’ve ever driven to Disneyland, you know that parking is a challenge. When the parks open each morning, long lines clog the nearby streets as engines idle, families waiting anxiously to enter the parking structure so they can start their day at the parks.

Parking attendants can only do so much to handle the tens of thousands of cars arriving every day at the Disneyland Resort. But what if a cutesy autonomous robot from Pixar’s Cars series could help direct traffic flow and guide you right into your parking spot?

That’s a project being tested with FieldAI, a company that builds the AI brains for robots. In a demo video at the Disney Accelerator Demo Day on Tuesday, Disney and FieldAI showed footage of robots that would assist with guiding cars through the parking process.

“Imagine if a character from Cars or robots from Wall-E direct you where to park when you arrive,” Gary Daniels, senior vice president of products and experiences at Disney Experiences Technology, said. “The work we are doing now is a great way to see how the robots function, and, as important, how people respond.”

Other companies build the robots; FieldAI slaps its physical AI solution in a box on top of them, having worked so far with around 30 different robot types, shapes and sizes. The box is equipped with multiple cameras that serve as the robot’s “eyes and ears,” helping the AI model process what it’s experiencing in real time. The robots also collect data while operating.

During the event at Walt Disney Studios, FieldAI showcased a Boston Dynamics robot dog and a miniature version of the BBX droids from The Mandalorian and Grogu that roam Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge at Disneyland. FieldAI-enabled robots have already been deployed in Disneyland at Galaxy’s Edge on the BBX droids, though they hedged that this is in its early stages.

“Our intelligence is on the bigger version and operating in the park already,” FieldAI CEO Ali Agha told reporters.

David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me it could also be used on characters that interact with guests at parks, naming Olaf and The Hulk as examples.

Another project with Disney involves getting multiple robots to talk to each other to coordinate missions.

Headquartered in Irvine, California, with offices in the San Francisco Bay Area, Boston and Pittsburgh, FieldAI primarily works in construction environments and energy facilities to complete tasks like inspections, material transport and supporting construction. But this is easily translated to a theme park environment, where paths and crowds are constantly changing, and autonomous robots need to account for that without needing mapping or GPS.

“Our BBX proof of concept explores how to bring that navigation together with Disney character performance,” said Doug Fidaleo, lab director, Disney Research, Walt Disney Imagineering R&D. “That’s what drew us to FieldAI: deep experience deploying robots in demanding, unstructured environments with uneven terrain, changing layouts and unexpected obstacles.”

Some of the use cases Agha gives include robots supporting security, perimeter patrols, helping cast members backstage and enabling more in-park experiences — even delivering items to people waiting in line for a ride.

“This is a highly self-autonomous system that operates without a positioning system,” Agha said.

Physical Intelligence (Pi) is another company that builds AI brains for robots. Also showcased during Disney’s Accelerator Demo Day, Pi is focused less on roaming droids that can help or entertain guests and instead on robots helping Disney cast members with backstage tasks.

Namely: picking up, folding, cleaning and sorting the 3D glasses used for rides like Toy Story Midway Mania and shows like Mickey’s PhilharMagic.

It’s an unpleasant task that’s a major pain point for cast members who have to spend a long time in a small room completing it several times a day. It also requires “dexterous manipulation,” with Pi previously working on general-purpose robots that perform tasks like folding and stacking, using robots that have grippers rather than five-digit hands.

Sourish Jasti, a technical staffer with Pi, said the company recently spent 12 days at Disneyland between midnight and 6 a.m. collecting data, testing logistics and moving its robots in and out of the park to see whether it could help with sorting the 3D glasses.

“This was like a robot internship,” Jasti said, adding that physical AI is like a toddler, in that it learns from actually doing things.

The robots — which, much like FieldAI, Pi doesn’t build but instead installs the brains for — could be either a humanoid on wheels or just a mechanical arm. There are cameras on the base and cameras on the wrists to help the AI model “see” what it’s doing as it picks up and sorts the glasses.

“We intend to have robots interning in many different spaces with Disney,” Jasti said, pointing to not only the theme parks but also Disney’s studios, hotel rooms and cruise liners, which he calls “mini cities.”

For both Pi and FieldAI, Min said the benefit is that using AI can train the robots much faster to do the tasks Disney needs them to do — and that going to companies like these, which are already well-established in fields like construction and manufacturing, makes it easier to transfer those skills to the theme parks.

Whether they’re roaming around parking structures or lands, or backstage helping workers, the AI-equipped autonomous robots are solving problems for Disney.

“The connection is through the core capabilities that we’re developing for our robots,” Fidaleo said. “Robots that can perceive the world around them, can act in the physical world and adapt when things change.”

Disney is continuing to push technology from the audio-animatronic figures used on rides like Pirates of the Caribbean, making them more sophisticated to build an immersive experience.

“From the expressive Na’vi shaman to a robotic Spider-Man flying through the air, to a walking baby Groot, each advance changes how we can experience a character in the physical world,” Fidaleo said. “The park of the future will be teeming with robot characters.”

#3210. I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro – and it’s the fastest Android I’ve ever seen

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If it's possible to release a flagship phone while at the same time making it appear more like a midrange phone, Red Magic has found a way.

RedMagic just announced the international launch of the RedMagic 12 Pro — its latest flagship phone. Typically, the company releases devices in China first and then slowly rolls them out to the rest of the world. This time around, the company knew it had a phone that could compete with other flagship devices.

Also: I’ve been a Google Pixel fan for years, but this $500 Android phone is giving me pause

RedMagic’s phones are high-performance devices known to do one thing especially well: mobile gaming. The RedMagic 12 Pro is no exception. It houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 CPU with up to 5.01 GHz, which is paired with the RedMagic R5 Gaming Chipset, and I can honestly say it’s the fastest Android phone I’ve ever tested.

After the initial setup, I installed Geekbench 7 to benchmark the phone and compare it to my Pixel 9 Pro. As for the latest iPhone, according to Geekbench, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes out ahead in single-core performance, but it just barely falls behind in multi-core performance.

The RedMagic 7 Pro nearly doubled the Pixel 11 Pro’s multi-core score. And Google’s device couldn’t beat the single-core score either. As I said, I’ve never seen a Geekbench score this high.

Real-world usage confirms these numbers, because the phone reacts faster and behaves more smoothly than any Android device I’ve owned or tested. It’s so smooth and fast, it feels like magic. But it’s not just the speed that makes this phone special.

First off, I’ve always liked RedMagic’s Android “skin.” As you use it, it seems to be some amalgamation of Android and iOS. RedMagic is essentially doing what Google’s been trying for years: making the smoothest possible animations on Android.

Also: I switched to an Android with liquid cooling for a week – now I wish every phone had it

The interface is as elegant as any I’ve seen on a mobile device. Pull down the notification shade, and it glides down like it was made of silk. Tap on an app launcher, and it opens immediately. Switch between apps, and there’s zero lag or jitter. On top of that, there’s hardly any bezel to speak of — the display goes nearly to the edge of the device.

There’s also no indication of where the front-facing camera is. There’s no pinhole (as you’ll find with many Android devices), and there’s no island (like on iPhones). It’s just a solid display with no interruptions.

The Pro 12 also feels really good in the hand. Both the back and the front are glass. Yes, it invites fingerprints, but it feels so smooth. The back of the phone also has that typical RedMagic look and feel with integrated RGB lighting zones. You can customize the lighting zones for things like fan on/off, game key atmosphere, media atmosphere, incoming calls, charging, and the alarm clock.

Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

The RedMagic 12 Pro is 100% a gaming phone. I installed “Diablo: Immortal” and found it to perform better than the last RedMagic gaming-specific tablet I tested. Not only was it fast, but the graphics were gorgeous. Crisp, smooth, and responsive.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

On this powerful gaming phone, you’ll find apps like Puzzle Spark, Mahjong Blast, Bolt Twist, GoGo! Blast, and Little Kitty, Big City preinstalled. These are not serious games. In fact, these game titles sound more like they belong on a list of malicious apps (they aren’t).

Also: This 9-inch tablet singlehandedly changed my mind about gaming on Android

I would rather see the Red Magic 12 Pro have zero preinstalled games than the collection it ships with. Yes, you can easily delete those apps, but their being on the phone kind of cheapens it. Given how amazing this phone is, I think RedMagic could get away with shipping a bit less cheese, and a lot more wine.

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

#3207. Cult Phone-Maker Nothing’s Mystery Screenless AI Device Is Coming Next Month

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Nothing CEO Carl Pei believes your work tools can be cool too. He's building one to prove it.

In the introduction to the essay published on X by Nothing CEO Carl Pei on Wednesday, it almost sounds like he’s arguing against the premise of standalone AI devices.

In Pei’s post, he suggests AI’s “iPhone moment” is still several years away. This could read as though Nothing is holding its horses rather than diving into the fray right now. But that isn’t the case; in fact, it’s quite the opposite.

“Our first AI-native product ships next month,” Pei says. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app.”

Pei is playing it characteristically coy. He’s dropping clues, and you can bet there will be more to come in the ensuing days and weeks up until the official launch of this mystery product.

Standalone AI devices are a burgeoning industry, even if they’re yet to result in a hugely compelling, must-have consumer product. Whether it be pins, pendants, glasses, headphones or tabletop devices, tech companies are flooding the market with new native AI devices. Some companies, such as OpenAI, are working on ideas behind closed doors, whereas others, such as AI note-taking experts Plaud, are already establishing a strong and loyal customer base.

British startup Nothing is predominantly known for its retro-inspired audio products and cool smartphones, around which the company is building a cult following as an alternative to more mainstream, generic phone companies. It’s more closely aligned with lifestyle and fashion brands than most of its tech brethren. In spite of this, it sounds like its first AI device will be more work than play.

Just like computers, AI will need to prove itself in the realm of productivity — the workplace — before it spills over into being truly useful and appreciated in our personal lives, writes Pei. And so, Nothing is building a tool for the workplace, albeit one with the company’s customary design-forward approach.

“We were taught that seriousness and beauty could not share a room,” says Pei. But he wants you to know that work tools can be beautiful, and he promises Nothing’s will be.

This is all very mysterious — perhaps more so because the image accompanying Pei’s post actually looks like it could be a snapshot of one of many different smartphones from the past decade or more. The simple black rectangle with one rounded corner looks distinctly unlike a Nothing device, and something a less imaginative tech company might produce.

We shouldn’t be fooled by this, though. Nothing has yet to bore us with a design, and it seems unlikely to start now — especially after Pei’s treatise on the subject. No doubt there will be more hints forthcoming, as Nothing gears up to persuade you that its products belong just as much in your office as at a warehouse rave in Berlin, and that its approach to AI is essential to your workflow above and beyond the offerings of its strait-laced competitors.

#3206. Is Claude Code truly faster with message threads? I did the math on my logs

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Claude Code’s update could save you time during demanding, hours-long coding sessions at no extra cost. But by how much? Here's my real-world result.

Anthropic yesterday introduced message threads as part of Claude’s Messages API. Don’t confuse message threads with traditional human-to-human discussion threads. With message threads, entire conversations no longer have to be resent with each API call, saving roughly 35% of time-to-first-token when Claude requests contain 500,000 to 1 million tokens.

This feature is on by default for most Claude Code users. API users can turn it on using the “thread” parameter for API requests.

Token consumption remains unchanged, so this capability doesn’t provide a cost savings. The 35% savings is Anthropic’s measurement.

Also: Claude Code’s revised projects adds AI orchestration, but local developers must wait

Timing data from roughly 980 turns in my own Claude Code logs before this feature became available shows that Claude usually began a response about 3 seconds after each mid-task request when running contexts of 500,000 tokens and up. During five busy evenings last month, my conversations made roughly 100 to 225 model calls in a four hour stretch.

Using Anthropic’s reported 35% median time-to-first token reduction in a quick projection, Claude estimated a 2- to 4-minute savings per four hour work session.

Agents often send a bunch of requests to the model during each conversation. Before message threads, each message sent the entire conversation with each request.

Imagine if you’re in a very long texting chat with a friend. Now imagine if every time you sent a text to that friend, you also had to send every other text and every other reply along with that original text. That’s how model messaging has always worked. Except now, with message threads, there’s a better way.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code – here’s why they choose it over Codex

With message threads turned on, agents only have to send what’s changed since the last turn. This reduces the amount of data transmission and increases responsiveness, what Anthropic calls time-to-first-token.

The benefit is seen most strongly in sessions that have a context of 500,000 to a 1 million tokens. About half of my sessions hit that context ceiling multiple times a night.

Anthropic reports that Claude’s message threads reduce median time-to-first-token by 35% for large requests. While my estimated savings of several minutes per session isn’t huge, the benefit increases with very long-running coding agents, and agents that transmit documents and image-heavy workloads.

For computer-using agents, all those screenshots “stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn,” according to the Anthropic blog post on the feature.

Also: How I made a paid Mac app in 11 days with Claude – without writing a single line of code

While the time savings may not seem huge, in larger enterprise deployments or deployments where you want the AI to respond faster, any reduction in latency is a big deal and will be seen in any application of Claude technology that has a lot of back-and-forth turns with large data payloads.

Even though the addition of threads to the Messages API can reduce latency, token usage and therefore cost won’t go down. That’s because the model itself will still process the full conversation during every turn. Rate limits also don’t change.

Message threads and prompt caching can work together to reduce workload. Prompt caching has been around for about two years now, and it does save money. That’s because prompt caching allows the model to avoid re-processing prompts over and over (for example, in looping analysis calls).

On the other hand, the message threads capability does offer an extra smidge of performance, at no extra cost. So, there’s that.

Context is the size of the full session that Claude is currently working with. The rough human equivalent is current working or short-term memory. Most Claude Code sessions max out at a million token context, where a locally-hosted AI on my 128GB Mac Studio handles a context no bigger than 64K, or about 6% of the Claude Code context size.

Also: After the vibe-coding rush comes the debugging hangover

Compaction is a process where the AI attempts to reduce and eliminate extra information to fit the current session’s turns into the available context. An oversimplified analog is when you save a JPEG with quality turned way down in order to save space. You lose a lot of the visual fidelity, but you still get the main idea.

The larger the context you have, the longer you can go before the session has to initiate compaction. But there’s a gotcha. The larger the context you have, the more chance there is the model will lose track of what it’s working on or make reasoning errors.

Individual one-off requests also won’t see an improvement from message threads. Also, any conversation that delays longer than 5 minutes between turns will send the full message contents and not just the new stuff.

This feature doesn’t eliminate context management or compaction. But if your context is quite large, it will make responses a bit snappier.

Overall, message threads are a good thing, a solid if small innovation that increases responsiveness. While the feature doesn’t reduce costs, there’s also no additional cost for the additional performance, which is itself a win.

#3205. GEO Group (GEO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Adelanto sale proceeds funded a major debt cut and a bigger buyback program.

The GEO Group, Inc. (GEO -8.57%) reported record-breaking quarterly financial performance, achieving its highest-ever levels of quarterly revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Management stated that the results were driven by the activation of new facility contracts signed in 2025 and an expanded scope of services for federal agencies. The company completed the $950 million sale of the Adelanto complex to the federal government while retaining a multiyear contract to provide support services at the site. This divestiture enabled the redemption of $650 million in senior secured notes, significantly reducing corporate debt and lowering net leverage to approximately 1.0 times Adjusted EBITDA. Management also increased its share repurchase authorization to $1.25 billion, signaling a shift in capital allocation toward shareholder returns as the company transitions toward a support services-focused business model.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the GEO Group Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in a listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then 1 on a touch tone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then 2. Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Pablo Paez, Executive Vice President of Corporate Relations. Please go ahead.

Zoley, Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and Founder and Shayn March, senior vice president and chief financial officer. This afternoon, we will discuss our third quarter results as well as our outlook. We will conclude the call with a question-and-answer session. This conference call is also being webcast live on our Investor website at investors.geogroup.com. Today, we will discuss non GAAP basis information. A reconciliation from non GAAP basis information to GAAP basis results is included in the press release and the supplemental disclosure we issued this morning.

Additionally, much of the information we will discuss today including the answers we give in response to your questions, may include forward looking statements. Regarding our beliefs and current expectations with respect to various matters. These forward looking statements are intended to fall within the safe harbor provisions of the securities laws. Our actual results may differ materially from those in the forward looking statements, as a result of various factors, contained in our Securities and Exchange Commission filings including the Form 10-Ks, 10-Q, and 8-K reports. With that, please allow me to turn this call over to our Chairman, CEO and Founder, George C. Zoley. George?

George C. Zoley: Thank you, Pablo, and good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Our diversified business units have continued to deliver strong financial and operational performance through 2026. And our third quarter 2026 results marked a record breaking quarter for GEO. Compared to the same period in 2026, our third quarter 2020 revenues increased 12% to approximately $761.1 million. While our third quarter 2026 net income attributable to GEO operations was approximately $49.2 million. Compared to the same period in 2025 our third quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA increased 21% to approximately $145.3 million. And our adjusted net income increased 48% to approximately $51.8 million.

These results represent the highest level of quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA ever reported in our company's history. Even better than expected performance in 2026 has been driven by the significant revenue growth from the new contracts that we entered into throughout 2025. They included the activation of 4 facilities to house ICE detainees totaling 6 thousand beds. Valued at approximately $280 million in annual revenues. So far in 2026, we have had an even more successful year for the new expanded services entering into new contracts for the activation of 4 additional facilities to house ICE detainees totaling approximately 4.8 thousand beds.

These contracts, along with the expanded scope of services at existing facilities created an overall value of approximately $500 million in incremental annual revenues. First, we entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 1.19 thousand-bed Bighorn facility in Hudson, Colorado while also entering into a lease agreement with the facility owner. The Bighorn support services contract is expected to generate approximately $85 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations. Starting in the first quarter of 2027.

We then entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center in the geo owned 1.32 thousand-bed Rivers facility in Winton North Carolina. The Rivers support services contract is expected to generate approximately $80 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations, also starting in the first quarter of 2027. More recently, we announced earlier this week the city of Big Spring in Texas has entered into a 10 year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 2.33 thousand-bed Big Spring complex comprised of 1.4 thousand-bed flight line facility and the 925-bed Cedar Hills facility.

GEO will provide support services at the Big Spring complex which is expected to generate approximately $200 million in annual revenues for GEO in the first full year of operations. Starting in the second quarter of 2027. Under all 3 of these contracts, ICE will reimburse GEO for the capital expenditures needed to reactivate these 4 facilities as well as providing funding for start up expenses during the activation period. Following the activation of these 4 facilities, our total ICE beds under contract will increase to approximately 33 thousand beds at 29 facilities. The current census across our active ICE facilities is approximately 24 thousand representing approximately 1/3 of the current national ICE population of approximately 73 thousand.

Over the past 2 quarters, we have also entered into new or modified contracts for the continued provision of support services at existing ICE processing centers. First, during the third quarter, we entered into a contract modification to increase staffing levels at the 1.94 thousand-bed Adelanto ICE processing center to support the increase in the scope of services at the facility adding $60 million in incremental annual revenues. More recently, last week, we announced that we have entered into a new 10 year management contract with expanded support services at incremental annual revenue value of $50 million at the GEO owned 1.64 thousand-bed Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington.

The new 10-year contract is expected to generate approximately $140 million in total annual revenues for GEO and continue through 10/27/2036, making it the first contract we have entered into ICE with a full base term of 10 years. This new contract was awarded under ongoing procurement that involves 3 other geo owned facilities, the Aurora facility, the Moshannon Valley facility, and Broward ICE Processing Center. Which are also expected to receive new 10-year contract awards. ICE enforcement initiatives nationwide are supported by significant funding that has already been approved by the United States Congress. ICE was allocated $45 billion for the detention under the 1 big beautiful bill which is available through 9/30/2029.

We believe that less than $10 billion of $45 billion has been spent so far. Under the Secure America Act, ICE also received $38.5 billion in baseline appropriations funding as well as an additional $30 billion for other priorities under the 1 Big Beautiful bill all of which is also available through 9/30/2029. As ICE continues to pursue these enforcement initiatives, we expect GEO to continue to be part of the solution as a 40-year partner to the agency. Following our recent contract announcements, we now have approximately 2.9 thousand idle beds that remain available at 4 company owned facilities, which are well suited for the needs of the federal government.

At full capacity, these 2.9 thousand idle beds could generate approximately $170 million in combined incremental revenues. Additionally, we have expansion capacity of several thousands of beds at existing geo managed ICE facilities. Our third quarter 2026 results also reflect a significant expansion in our secure transportation services on behalf of ICE, and the US Marshals Service. As a result of new or amended contracts we entered into in 2025. The support services that we provide under ICE Air transportation subcontract have continued To Steadily Grow Driven By The Increase In The Number Of Removable Flights.

Additionally, Our New Bighorn Rivers and Big Spring contracts with ICE are expected to generate approximately $28 million in combined additional annual transportation services revenues once normalized in 2027. Importantly, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, our ISAP contract continued to experience a steady technology shift to more intensive and higher price monitoring devices such as ankle monitors. ISAP is the only ICE program currently in place to provide electronic monitoring and case management services for individuals on the non-detained docket.

The program relies on several forms of monitoring including GPS ankle bracelets, or wrist worn devices that provide real time tracking as well as the SmartLink phone app, which relies on facial recognition voice ID, and GPS to confirm a person's location during the predetermined check-in. The current overall ISAP count is approximately 190 thousand participants up from 184 thousand participants 3 months ago. The number is 58 thousand currently, from 17 thousand early in 2025. We also continue to experience a steady increase in the number of ISAP participants assigned to case management services, which involves staff interaction and monitoring for approximately 121 thousand individuals currently.

As a result of these trends, revenue and net operating income for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period a year ago, reversing a multiyear trend of revenue and net operating income declines. Additionally, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, we generated revenues of approximately $3 million from our skip tracing contract. Moving to our outlook, we have increased our net income and adjusted EBITDA guidance for 2026 to reflect the strength of our results in the first 3 quarters of the year. Our fourth quarter 2020 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance exceeds our third quarter 2 thousand and 26 results.

Positioning GEO to set another record breaking quarter. Looking forward to 2027, there are several sources of future upside compared to our 2026 guidance. They include the expected activation of 4 new ICE facilities at Bighorn, Rivers, and the Big Spring Complex. Comprised of 2 facilities. Additional growth in our additional secure services segment from the reactivation of additional idle facilities and or higher overall populations across our active facilities. The expected transition of our previously announced managed only contracts for the 1.88 thousand-bed Graceville facility and the 985-bed Bay facility in the state of Florida, which are expected to occur on 07/01/2027.

Additional volume increases and/or accelerated technology service mix in our ISAP contract, additional growth in our secured transportation services business, and additional revenue from higher utilization of our skip tracing contracts. Before I turn the call over to our CFO, Shayn March for a more detailed review of our third quarter results and guidance I would like to provide you with an update regarding the plan by ICE and DHS to purchase existing privately owned turnkey ICE processing centers. As we announced last month, we completed the sales of our 1.28 thousand-bed Adelanto West ICE processing center 660-bed Adelanto East, 704-bed Desert View Annex to DHS.

For an aggregate gross sales price of $950 million and net proceeds after taxes and transaction fees and expenses of approximately $705 million. We expect to continue providing support services at the Adelanto complex under our existing contract with ICE, which has a full effective term through 12/19/2034. We used proceeds from the sales of the Adelanto complex for the redemption of our $650 million 2029 senior secured notes and we also entered into an amended and restated credit agreement extending the maturity of our $550 million revolving credit facility to July 2031. And also increasing our restricted pay payment capacity, including share repurchases.

Following the redemption of the 2029 senior secured notes, our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. As we previously announced, our Board of Directors has increased our share repurchase authorization, which is effective through 12/31/2029 by $750 million to $1.25 billion. Based on our current leverage and so long as we remain below specified leverage levels, GEO is permitted to make unlimited restricted payments, including share repurchases under both the amended credit facility agreement and the senior unsecured note indenture.

Given the intrinsic value of our assets including 48 thousand owned beds, our strong financial performance in providing diversified secured support services and our expected future growth we believe that our stock continues to be significantly undervalued and offers a very attractive investment opportunity. Therefore, in addition to further debt reduction and other general corporate purposes, we intend to allocate a substantial portion of future facility sales proceeds and recurring free cash flow toward our expanded share repurchase authorization, which may include structured share repurchases on an accelerated basis. Following the recently completed asset sales, ICE now uses approximately 34 existing detention sites nationwide that are owned and operated by private contractors.

CoreCivic now owns and operates approximately 12 ICE detention facilities. While GEO owns and operates 20 ICE detention facilities. In addition to the facility sales we completed last month, we remain engaged in active processes for the sale of multiple other company owned facilities to ICE subject to mutual agreement on price and GEO's continued management of those facilities under long term support services contract. We believe we have 2 types of assets, the building and the businesses of providing support services. We are pursuing additional potential sales of the buildings but we want to retain the business of providing support services.

We continue to consider ourselves primarily a support services operator and will place particular importance on our ability to continue our support services at any additional facilities sold to ICE. Specifically, we believe that our current active negotiations could result in additional sales before the end of 2026 for up to 4 additional facilities. We believe that the future sales are likely to have similar valuations to the transactions that have already been completed by ICE. With standard adjustments with respect to geography, facility size, and age. And it is possible that the number of facilities targeted for acquisition by ICE could continue to grow in the future.

At this time, there is no definitive agreement in place and no precise timeline for the closing of any additional transactions. And GEO can provide no assurance that any additional transactions will in fact occur. While the exact timing of government actions is always difficult to estimate, we remain focused on pursuing new growth opportunities and allocating capital to enhance long term value for our shareholders. At this time, I will turn the call over to Shayn to review our quarterly results and increase guidance.

Shayn March: Thank you, George. Good afternoon, everyone. The third quarter of 2026 set all time highs for GEO in quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA, and also an all time high in quarterly adjusted net income under a non REIT corporate structure. Revenues for the third quarter of 2026 increased by approximately $761.1 million up from approximately $682.3 million for the prior year's third quarter. Reflecting a 12% increase. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported net income attributable to GEO operations of approximately $49.2 million or $0.37 per diluted share. This compares to net income attributable to GEO operations of approximately $173.9 million or $1.24 per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Which included the $228 million gain on the sale of the Lund, Oklahoma facility. Adjusting for unusual and nonrecurring items, third quarter 2026 adjusted net income increased to approximately $51.8 million or $0.39 per diluted share up from approximately $35 million or $0.25 per diluted share in the prior year's third quarter. Our adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 increased to approximately $145 million up from approximately $120.1 million in the prior year's third quarter reflecting a 21% increase. Driving this historical quarterly performance, our owned and leased secured services revenues increased by approximately $46 million or 13% compared to prior year's third quarter.

This increase was driven by the activation of 3 company owned facilities under new contracts with ICE, which was partly offset by revenue lost from the sale of the Lawton Oklahoma facility. Quarterly revenues for our managed only contracts increased by approximately $31 million or 19% from the prior year's third quarter. This increase was primarily driven by the joint venture agreement for the management of the North Florida detention facility, as well as certain transportation revenue increases that are reported in this segment. Quarterly revenues for our owned and leased reentry services increased by approximately $3.5 million partly offset by a $3 million decline in nonresidential services revenues compared to the prior year's third quarter.

Finally, third quarter 26 revenues for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased by approximately 1.6% compared to the third quarter of 25, reversing a multiyear trend of quarterly revenue declines for this important segment and demonstrating the strength of the continued favorable technology and case management mix shift in our ISAP contract, which more than offset some price reductions previously reported. Turning to expenses. During the third quarter of 2026, our operating expenses increased by approximately 8.5% as a result of the activation of our ICE facility contracts and increased occupancy compared to prior year's third quarter. Our general and administrative expenses for the third quarter of 2026 increased modestly to approximately 9.5% of revenue.

Approximately 9.1% of the prior year's third quarter revenue the result of additional business development expenses. Our third quarter 26 net interest expense remained steady at approximately $36 million compared to the prior year's third quarter. Our effective tax rate for the third quarter of 2026 was approximately 27%. Moving to our outlook. We have updated our guidance for the fourth quarter and the full year 2026. For the fourth quarter of 2026, we have increased our GAAP net income guidance to a range of $591 million to $595.5 million which includes the gain on the sale of the Adelanto, California ICE complex.

We have also increased fourth quarter 2026 adjusted net income guidance to a range of $46 million to $51 million or a range of $0.35 to $0.39 per diluted share on a quarterly revenue of $777 million to $827 million We have increased our fourth quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $149 million to $154 million If this guidance is achieved, the fourth quarter of 2026 would set another record breaking quarter for GEO. While also positioning our company for a strong 2027 outlook.

For the full year 2026, we have increased GAAP net income guidance to a range of $726.3 million to $730.5 million which includes the gain on sale of the Adelanto, California, ICE complex in the fourth quarter of 2026. This represents a 56% increase over 2025 adjusted net income at the midpoint of $187.5 million We have increased our full year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $568 million to $573 million representing a 23% increase at the midpoint of $570.5 million We expect total unreimbursed capital expenditures for the full year 2026 to be between $140 million and $150 million and expect normal unreimbursed CapEx to decline to approximately $100 million in 2027. Moving to our balance sheet.

Following the sale of the Adelanto complex in October, we completed the redemption of our $650 million senior secured notes and executed an amendment to our $550 million revolving credit facility extending its maturity and increasing our restricted payments capacity including share repurchases. Our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. Our available liquidity is approximately $600 million including cash on hand and revolver availability. Net of cash, our current leverage is approximately 1x adjusted EBITDA, And based on our current outlook, we have reset our capital strategy to remain at or below this net leverage level going forward.

Based on our current leverage and so long as we remain below specified leverage levels, GEO is permitted to make unlimited restricted payments including share repurchases under both the amended credit facility agreement and the senior unsecured note indenture. Given what I believe is a significant discount in our stock valuation, our Board of Directors previously reported, increased our share repurchase authorization which is effective through 12/31/2029, by $750 million to $1.25 billion We plan to remain active under this program regardless of future asset sales. At this time, will turn the call back to George.

Which are expected to transition on 07/01/2027. The additional volume increases and or accelerated technology and service mix in our ISAP contract. Additional growth in our secured transportation services business, and additional revenue from higher utilization of our skip tracing contracts. Having already completed the sale of the Adelanto complex for $950 million, we believe it is possible that up to 4 additional facilities owned by GEO could be sold in the fourth quarter of 2026. These potential asset sales would represent another significant liquidity and shareholder value creation event for our company. Given the intrinsic value of our assets, 48 thousand owned beds, our strong financial performance in providing diversified secure support services and our expected future growth. #3204. Your Monitoring Stack Isn’t The Problem. The Detection-To-Ownership Gap Is

Judit Sharon is the founder and CEO of OnPage Corporation, an advanced, secure critical communication and collaboration platform provider.

​At 2:07 a.m., a monitoring platform detects that a customer-facing application is failing. It creates a ticket, sends an email and posts to an operations channel. At 2:19 a.m., no engineer has taken ownership of the incident.

The monitoring system did its job. The response process did not.

Detection-to-ownership time is the elapsed time between detecting a critical incident and a qualified responder acknowledging and accepting responsibility for it. Unlike mean time to detect (MTTD), detection-to-ownership time measures the human-response gap after monitoring has already identified the problem.

For CIOs, IT operations leaders and site reliability teams, those 12 minutes represent a distinct failure: The organization knew something was wrong, but no one was responsible for acting on it.

Alert delivery does not guarantee incident ownership because delivery confirms that a notification reached a destination, not that a qualified responder saw it, accepted responsibility or began acting on it.

An alert may reach a shared inbox nobody is watching. A Slack or Microsoft Teams notification can disappear into routine conversation. Email-to-text gateways provide another notification path, but they may still fail to get attention. An answering service can also delay ownership while it determines urgency and locates the on-call responder.

The mistake is assuming that, because a notification went out, the right responder has taken charge. To see where the handoff breaks down, distinguish five states:

• Detected: A system identified the problem.

• Delivered: The alert reached its intended destination.

• Read: The responder has seen the critical alert.

• Owned: A qualified responder has acknowledged the incident and accepted responsibility for the next action.

• Resolved: The issue was addressed, with the alert status synced back to the originating system where supported.

Delivery is not ownership. For a critical incident, “someone received it” is not enough; the team needs to know who read the alert and took ownership, when and what happened next.

An event should trigger an immediate page when it has meaningful business or customer impact, requires timely human intervention and the responder can act on it.

IT and digital operations teams need telemetry, warnings and diagnostic information, but not every event warrants immediate interruption. When routine conditions and genuine failures arrive with the same urgency, responders discount the signal and alert noise becomes alert fatigue.

Set stricter paging criteria. A customer-facing outage, a failed payment workflow or a major security event may require immediate response. A transient warning that clears without intervention may belong in a dashboard or ticket queue.

The distinction should depend on business impact, service criticality and whether the responder can take useful action. A page-worthy alert should clearly state what service is affected, what failed and where the responder should go next. It should also stand out, override silent mode when required and persist until someone responds.

On-call schedules and escalation policies reduce response time by automatically routing critical alerts to the person currently responsible and escalating when that responder does not acknowledge the incident within a defined period.

Static contact lists and manual routing can slow response when people change roles, take leave or rotate through on-call shifts. Schedule-based routing directs the alert to whoever is currently responsible. Round-robin routing can distribute incidents across several qualified responders while preserving individual ownership.

To keep critical pages meaningful, teams can use deduplication, suppression or brief delays for conditions likely to clear on their own. A workflow might begin with SMS, email or a phone call, followed by a persistent mobile page if no one responds. More urgent incidents may warrant immediate paging and automatic escalation.

Consider a database supporting a customer-facing application that becomes unavailable. Monitoring detects the failure and pages the assigned on-call engineer. If that engineer does not read the incident within the defined interval, the alert escalates to the next responder. The notification path continues until someone qualified assumes responsibility.

Automation does not make the technical decisions needed to resolve the incident. Engineers still diagnose and resolve the problem. Automation removes avoidable delay in getting the right person involved.

Slack and Microsoft Teams help coordinate incidents. A channel notification alone, however, does not establish who must respond.

Posting to a channel tells a group something happened. Paging assigns responsibility to a specific responder and creates an escalation path if that person doesn’t respond.

Integrations into on-call management and alerting workflows can reduce context switching by allowing teams to initiate a paging workflow from the Slack or Teams conversation where an incident is already being discussed.

Whether these practices work should be visible in the data. Detection-to-ownership time starts when the system identifies the incident and ends when a qualified person accepts responsibility. Teams can break that interval into delivery time, acknowledgment time and confirmed ownership.

Those measures reveal different problems. Fast delivery but slow acknowledgment may point to alert noise, alert fatigue or ineffective notification methods. Quick acknowledgment without clear ownership suggests unclear responsibilities. Frequent escalation may expose gaps in staffing or on-call coverage.

Testing matters, too. Test the workflow during shift changes, after hours and when the primary responder is unavailable. Test what happens when the first page goes unanswered.

Monitoring tells you what happened. An effective incident alert management process determines who needs to act, whether they received the alert, whether they responded and who owns the incident now.

If the organization already knows a critical service is failing but still cannot say who owns the response, faster monitoring will not close that gap.​

#3203. This clever banking scam keeps phishing by faking its own demise – how it works

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

You won't see the 'suspended' sign because it's not meant for you.

KELA researchers have exposed an active financial-scam infrastructure that hosts hundreds of fraudulent websites capable of faking their own suspensions to stay online. As of Oct. 25, 2026, 248 financial scam and phishing domains tied to 189 major US banks and financial services have been linked to the same infrastructure.

According to the cybersecurity firm’s report, published on Tuesday, the “Suspended” infrastructure operation runs websites that have cloned the official domains of victim organizations, with a particular focus on business banking. Many domains use the [keyword]-[bank].com format, slotting in keywords such as “secure,” “disable,” “protect,” and “cancel.”

Also: Beware of Bluetooth sniffers: How your favorite gadgets could be exposing your data

A handful of servers spread across two shared hosting providers run the backend of Suspended infrastructure, which has also been tied to phishing campaigns targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and government services in the UK, the Netherlands, Australia, and New Zealand. As a result, the researchers believe that either a single operator is behind the setup or that the server infrastructure is part of a wider phishing-as-a-service platform.

This phishing campaign stands out because of how the cybercriminals behind the scam are protecting it: by issuing takedown notices.

When you visit a website and see a message that it has been taken down or suspended, it’s usually because the domain has been associated with malicious or illegal activity, including phishing and scams. Law enforcement agencies, often with help from technology firms, find these websites, obtain the necessary court orders, and seize the infrastructure or accounts behind them to force a suspension through a registrar or hosting provider.

You see the notice, you move on — and this also goes for scanners and security teams.

However, in this case, the scam artists created a mechanism to show it themselves, to avoid being flagged and taken down. But it’s when they show it that matters.

The false suspension notice appears deceptively simple at first glance. A phishing kit embedded in the domain registers the IP address of each visitor, and on their second visit, they are shown a fake “account suspended” page. The kit is disguised as a challenge page similar to those legitimately used by Cloudflare.

Researchers also detected other decoys, including “Sorry, you’ve been blocked” notices, blank pages, and redirections to Google. Some pages also have reCAPTCHAs, and the researchers detected scripts that block browser developer tools, likely to slow analysis.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages – here’s how

But why show fake suspension notices in the first place? To scanners and cybersecurity teams, it looks like someone else has already dealt with the malicious domain, and they can move on to the next suspicious website.

“That design targets exactly the people who could shut a site down,” KELA says. “A victim typically follows a link once. A scanner, a security team or a takedown provider checks a reported site and then checks it again to confirm, and the second check shows what looks like a completed takedown.”

As shown in the image below, while scanners would detect a suspension notice, victims would still see the cloned website, complete with lures to entice them into entering their information, leading to financial fraud and potentially identity theft. After all, one visit is enough.

As of this writing, there are 248 live domains, plus those taken offline after the researchers disclosed their findings to law enforcement; over 300 scam domains have been hosted on the same infrastructure since May this year. Unfortunately, this phishing campaign remains active, with new domains appearing every day.

One lead could reveal the operator: a remote desktop connection to the malicious infrastructure through a standard UK home broadband connection, but it has not been verified.

Use a phishing link checker to verify whether a URL is trustworthy, and remember that any email or message claiming to be from your bank may be fraudulent.

When it comes to organizations, KELA has released a free Bank Phishing Check tool that compares official domains and organizations against the websites uncovered during the firm’s research.
